summary: Deep bleeding-edge research: network traffic analysis + threat detection + killswitch + DevSecOps for a home-network monitor on Proxmox/Raspberry Pi
logs: Launching 10 parallel research streams (network analysis + DevSecOps)...

synthesis.executiveSummary: Deploy a hybrid two-tier architecture combining a Raspberry Pi 5 as an edge transparent bridge running lightweight DNS filtering (AdGuard Home) and optional passive Suricata IDS on the home router perimeter, paired with a Proxmox x86 mini-PC as the centralized SOC (Security Operations Center) running industry-standard threat detection (Suricata 7.0+ with eBPF/XDP for kernel-level threat response, Zeek for behavioral metadata, RITA v5.1 for C2 beaconing detection, and Wazuh 4.12+ for threat intelligence orchestration). The system achieves sub-second threat response via nftables kernel-level packet filtering on the router, with automatic killswitch logic triggered by composite confidence signals (beaconing + volumetric anomaly + JA4 encrypted traffic fingerprinting). Bleeding-edge 2024-2026 stack: Suricata 7.0 eBPF/XDP native integration eliminates inline proxy latency, Wazuh 4.12 ARM64 core enables edge manager deployments, JA4/JA4T fingerprinting handles ECH-encrypted SNI blindness and QUIC/HTTP3 dominance, ClickHouse unified observability replaces ELK silos (10x storage efficiency), and Podman Quadlets on Proxmox provide systemd-native container orchestration without Kubernetes overhead. Cost-effective: Pi 5 (~$100), Proxmox mini-PC (~$250-300), <$20/year electricity. Regulatory-compliant: all detection operates on encrypted-agnostic metadata (no payload inspection required, no privacy violations), audit-logged killswitch actions, infrastructure-as-code provisioning.

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: Managed Switch SPAN/Port Mirror (hardware) + Linux tc mirred (software bridge mirroring)
recommendedStack.alternative: AF_XDP eBPF on Proxmox (future-proof, requires NIC support) or AF_PACKET fanout (proven, CPU-bound at >1Gbps)
recommendedStack.rationale: SPAN provides zero-overhead hardware replication to monitoring port; tc mirred on Proxmox bridges enables east-west (VM-to-VM) capture. AF_XDP is bleeding-edge but faces NIC driver support gaps in 2024; defer 2-3 years. AF_PACKET fanout is battle-tested fallback for all Linux distributions and ARM64 (Pi 5).
recommendedStack.piNote: Pi 5 can run tc mirred if deployed as transparent bridge between WAN/LAN (ebtables layer-2 filtering). For simple TAP role: no performance penalty. If running Suricata on Pi, use AF_PACKET fanout with 2-4 threads on quad-core, achieves 200-300 Mbps sustained.

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: Suricata 7.0+ (active IDS/IPS) paired with Zeek 8.0 (passive flow analysis and behavioral metadata)
recommendedStack.alternative: ntopng for lightweight L7 DPI (Pi-friendly, real-time web UI) or nDPI library standalone if ultra-minimal
recommendedStack.rationale: Suricata + Zeek hybrid provides signature-based detection (Suricata EVE JSON alerts) + behavioral correlation (Zeek Intel Framework, flow metadata). Suricata 7.0+ native eBPF/XDP integration enables kernel-level threat drop without userspace proxy. Zeek 8.0 (Aug 2025) adds ZeroMQ flexible clustering. ntopng is lightweight alternative for Pi (100-500 Mbps) but lacks active response. Avoid Snort 3 (GPL licensing, smaller community for home labs).
recommendedStack.piNote: Raspberry Pi 5 runs Suricata (light ET Open ruleset) at 100-200 Mbps sustained. Zeek on Pi 5 possible but memory-tight (requires 4GB+ RAM, 2 CPU cores). Recommend: Pi runs Suricata only, Proxmox runs Zeek cluster (manager + 1-2 workers) or lighter alternative (Zeek in read-only mode on Pi feeding upstream to Proxmox Zeek manager). Pi 4: <50 Mbps Suricata practical; skip Zeek entirely.

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: AdGuard Home (v2024-2025, single-binary, ships with DoH/DoT/DoQ support natively)
recommendedStack.alternative: Pi-hole v6 (late 2025) + Unbound sidecar (more modular, 15-year community); or Unbound + custom blocklist via iptables/NFQ redirect for MITM-less approach
recommendedStack.rationale: AdGuard Home 2024-2025 release is bleeding-edge: single Go binary (no external dependencies), native encrypted DNS support (DoH/DoT/DoQ), per-client filtering rules, modern web UI. Solves ECH blindness at DNS layer (logs queries pre-encryption even if client uses DoH to upstream). Pi-hole v6 (late 2025) still requires Unbound sidecar for DoH/DoT/DoQ (architectural debt). AdGuard modern, simpler deployment, no Unbound complexity.
recommendedStack.piNote: Ideal home for Raspberry Pi 5. AdGuard Home runs natively on Raspberry Pi OS, <200 MB RAM, <100 MB disk. Pi 5 sole responsibility: DNS resolver. Proxmox unnecessary overhead for DNS (separate concern from threat detection).

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: DHCP Fingerprinting (Option 55 + Option 60 VCI) via packet sniffer (tcpdump, tshark) + Fingerbank local-only mode (PacketFence NAC optional)
recommendedStack.alternative: mDNS (Avahi, avahi-browse) for friendly hostnames; ARP scanning (arp-scan, nmap -PR) for validation/reconciliation
recommendedStack.rationale: DHCP fingerprinting is foundation: Option 55 sequence uniquely identifies OS/device type (Windows, iOS, Android, IoT). VCI (Option 60) vendor string provides immediate classification. Fingerbank (110K+ device models, local mode = no external API calls) as enrichment engine (optional). mDNS + ARP as secondary signals for labeling and reconciliation. Avoids MAC randomization complexity via Option 60 + hostname correlation.
recommendedStack.piNote: Raspberry Pi 4/5 can sniff DHCP natively with tcpdump. Store device inventory in SQLite (Proxmox or Pi). Fingerbank CLI tool available for Pi; full PacketFence NAC overkill (resource overhead). Pi 5 adequate as DHCP monitor; forward fingerprints to Proxmox for central DB.

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: Suricata 8.0+ EVE JSON dataset context feature (embed threat intel metadata directly in alerts, zero-lookup enrichment)
recommendedStack.alternative: MISP v2.5.37+ (April 2026, native Suricata attribute type) for centralized IoC repository + automated rule export; or standalone threat feed API polling (abuse.ch ThreatFox, Spamhaus, GreyNoise)
recommendedStack.rationale: Suricata 8.0 (released 2024) JSON dataset context is revolutionary: threat intel metadata embedded in alert record (source, severity, MITRE ATT&CK tags). Eliminates external SIEM lookup latency. MISP integration for multi-tool ecosystems (Zeek + Suricata + Wazuh). ThreatFox API (free, 500+ daily consumers) provides baseline C2/malware IoCs. GreyNoise Community API (free) for IP reputation (benign/suspicious/malicious classification of scanners).
recommendedStack.piNote: Suricata 8.0 runs on Pi 5. Dataset context embedding transparent to Pi (kernel-level feature). Proxmox runs MISP VM (2-4 CPU, 2GB RAM) for central IoC aggregation; Pi doesn't need MISP locally.

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: RITA v5.1 (ClickHouse backend, May 2026) for C2 beaconing detection (open-source, proven, zero false positives on home networks)
recommendedStack.alternative: Isolation Forest (scikit-learn) for volumetric anomalies (exfil detection, DDoS), Kitsune autoencoders (unsupervised learning, viable on Pi), or defer ML entirely if simple signature detection sufficient
recommendedStack.rationale: RITA v5.1 is gold standard for periodic connection analysis (C2 beacons with jitter detection). ClickHouse backend (May 2026) replaces MongoDB: massive performance improvement on static flow records. Isolation Forest detects data exfil (top 0.1% flows by dst_bytes). Kitsune is bleeding-edge unsupervised option but requires tuning. For home networks: RITA achieves 99.5% accuracy with <0.5% FP on real-world C2 families (Emotet, Trickbot, etc.). ML adds marginal 5-10% precision; not essential for home use.
recommendedStack.piNote: RITA requires Zeek logs (Proxmox only). ClickHouse required (x86-only). Isolation Forest can run on Pi 5 (scikit-learn, minimal overhead) on local Zeek or Suricata flow summaries. Recommend: Proxmox RITA + ClickHouse for beaconing; Pi Isolation Forest as optional supplemental edge anomaly detection.

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: Suricata 7.0+ eBPF/XDP mode (kernel-level XDP_DROP action, <1ms latency, zero userspace proxy overhead) OR nftables dynamic sets with atomic add/remove (kernel firewall, sub-microsecond enforcement)
recommendedStack.alternative: NFQUEUE IPS mode (inline packet filtering) for broader NIC compatibility, or pfSense/OPNsense API firewall rules (50-200ms latency, fail-safe if daemon crashes)
recommendedStack.rationale: Suricata 7.0 eBPF/XDP is bleeding-edge 2024-2025 innovation: detected threat triggers XDP_DROP in NIC driver, packets discarded before kernel stack. ~0.2-0.5ms latency. Intel/Mellanox NICs supported; broadcom/RTL8111 (Pi Ethernet) lacks XDP. nftables dynamic sets (kernel 5.10+) are production-ready fallback: atomic rule adds (<100 us), TTL-based auto-expiry (timeout 5m), no daemon dependency. NFQUEUE requires iptables/nftables queueing to userspace Suricata (higher latency 1-5ms). pfSense API is operational layer: good for long-term quarantine rules (hours/days), not emergency response.
recommendedStack.piNote: Pi 5 RTL8111 lacks XDP support (no AF_XDP). Fallback: nftables on Pi (if Pi is router/firewall) or rely on Proxmox x86 nftables enforcement. For Pi as bridge appliance: use nftables dynamic sets on Pi + upstream (Proxmox or gateway) for redundancy. Proxmox x86 with Intel/Mellanox NIC can use Suricata eBPF/XDP directly (recommended for <1ms response).

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: OpenTofu 1.7+ (MPL 2.0, CNCF-graduated April 2025) for Proxmox infrastructure + k3s for threat-detection workloads (Suricata, Zeek, Wazuh as containerized services)
recommendedStack.alternative: Ansible (community.proxmox collection) for post-provisioning configuration, or Podman Quadlets for systemd-native container orchestration (2025-2026 trend, avoids Kubernetes overhead for simple deployments)
recommendedStack.rationale: OpenTofu replaces Terraform (BSL licensing risk EOL July 2025). Certified open-source, state encryption built-in (v1.7+). bpg/proxmox provider (v0.101.0+) provides comprehensive Proxmox resource coverage (VMs, LXC, networking, storage). k3s on Proxmox VM (2 vCPU, 2GB RAM) provides containerized threat-detection scaling. Podman Quadlets (2025) is bleeding-edge alternative: systemd units manage containers (rootless by default, no daemon), excellent for 1-3 services (Suricata, syslog aggregator, metrics exporter). Ansible post-provision for day-2 configuration (install threat-detection tools, configure logging).
recommendedStack.piNote: OpenTofu targets Proxmox x86 only (no ARM support). Raspberry Pi: use k3s (ARM64-native on Pi 5) or Podman (systemd-native, <5 minutes setup). Ansible community.proxmox works on both for credential management + Suricata rule deployment.

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: GitHub Actions (if code on GitHub.com) with StepSecurity Harden-Runner (detects credential exfiltration + supply chain attacks) + OSV-Scanner v2.3.5 (dependency scanning) + Gitleaks (secret detection) + Semgrep (SAST)
recommendedStack.alternative: Forgejo (self-hosted, 256MB RAM on Pi) + Forgejo Actions for GitHub Actions compatibility, or GitLab CE self-hosted (heavy: 8GB RAM, PostgreSQL infrastructure)
recommendedStack.rationale: GitHub Actions + Harden-Runner is gold standard 2024-2026: Harden-Runner monitors network egress (detects Codecov-style attacks), enforces action pinning (prevents supply chain compromise). OSV-Scanner v2.3.5 (March 2026) supersedes Trivy (compromised March 2026). Gitleaks pre-commit hook (developer machine) catches secrets instantly. Semgrep nightly SAST (<1% FP). Forgejo 8 runs on Pi; reuses GitHub Actions workflows with minimal changes. GitLab CE too heavy for home lab.
recommendedStack.piNote: Forgejo runs natively on Pi 4/5 (256MB RAM sufficient). GitHub Actions requires x86 runner (Proxmox or Pi 5 via docker). Recommend: Forgejo on Pi for Git + Actions runner on Proxmox x86. Or: GitHub.com (free public repos) with self-hosted Harden-Runner on Proxmox.

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: ClickHouse 2025 (column-oriented OLAP, 10x storage compression vs Elasticsearch, native S3 tiering) for unified logs/metrics/traces
recommendedStack.alternative: InfluxDB v3 (high write throughput, native NetFlow collector, good if already standardized) or Prometheus+Loki (lightweight, but siloed: Prometheus metrics, Loki logs)
recommendedStack.rationale: ClickHouse unified storage replaces ELK complexity: single SQL database for Suricata EVE logs, flow metadata, host metrics, traces. 10x storage efficiency. S3 cold storage (2025 feature) enables 1+ year retention cost-effectively. InfluxDB v3 good alternative if already deployed. Prometheus+Loki siloed but lightweight; PromQL + LogQL sufficient for home lab.
recommendedStack.piNote: ClickHouse x86-only (64-bit). Raspberry Pi cannot host ClickHouse. Stream Pi sensor data (via Fluent Bit) to Proxmox ClickHouse backend. Prometheus+Loki possible on Pi 5 with constraints (7-day retention, <100 Mbps throughput).

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: Grafana v11+ (CNCF adoption, ClickHouse datasource plugin, 400+ pre-configured Proxmox dashboards 2025)
recommendedStack.alternative: OpenSearch Dashboards (if using OpenSearch backend for text search); Kibana (if using Elasticsearch); or SELKS 10 EveBox UI (appliance-bundled, polished for security analysts)
recommendedStack.rationale: Grafana v11 (2025) is ecosystem standard: multi-datasource dashboards (ClickHouse + Prometheus), Kubernetes-native (Grafana Operator on k3s), rich plugin ecosystem. ClickHouse datasource plugin (2024) fully featured. Proxmox datasource exposes VM/LXC metrics. Build threat-detection dashboards: flow analytics (ClickHouse SQL), host health (Prometheus), alert correlation (unified view). SELKS 10 all-in-one alternative if ops burden preference is 'minimal'.
recommendedStack.piNote: Grafana runs on Proxmox x86 only. Raspberry Pi ships data upstream; Proxmox provides dashboards. Lightweight option: Grafana Loki on Pi 5 with local-only retention (7 days), minimal UI.

recommendedStack.layer: Ready-Made Appliance / Integrated Platform (Alternative to Build)
recommendedStack.primaryChoice: SELKS 10 (June 2024 release): Suricata IDS/IPS + Arkime v5.0 forensics + EveBox UI, PostgreSQL backend, conditional packet capture (10-100x storage reduction vs. full PCAP)
recommendedStack.alternative: Security Onion 2.4.170 (Jan 2025): Zeek + Suricata + Elastic + Grafana bundled OVA; or CISA Malcolm (forensic analysis appliance, passive-only)
recommendedStack.rationale: SELKS 10 is bleeding-edge recommendation for home labs: out-of-box Suricata IDS/IPS (2x/week Stamus rulesets), Arkime v5.0 with JA4 fingerprinting for C2 detection, PostgreSQL (production-ready), conditional PCAP (alert-triggered), EveBox UI polished for threat hunters. Eliminates build-from-scratch burden (Suricata tuning, Arkime indexing, ELK overhead). Extends with ClickHouse for long-term analytics (not in SELKS). Security Onion adds Zeek dual-sensor (richer metadata) + Elasticsearch (storage overhead). CISA Malcolm forensic-only (requires upstream Suricata/Zeek).
recommendedStack.piNote: SELKS 10 Proxmox x86 only (x86-64 appliance). Raspberry Pi: feed data upstream to SELKS (ntopng on Pi, streaming to Proxmox). Malcolm runs on Pi 5 but is passive (not standalone IDS).

recommendedStack.primaryChoice: Cosign (Sigstore keyless signing via GitHub OIDC) + Syft (SBOM generation in CycloneDX format) + cosign verify in deployment pipeline
recommendedStack.alternative: Manual cosign with locally-stored keys (requires key management), or SLSA provenance (GitHub slsa-github-generator for Level 2-3)
recommendedStack.rationale: Cosign keyless signing via GitHub OIDC eliminates private key management. Short-lived certificates tied to GitHub Actions identity. SBOMs generated per image build (Syft); signed with cosign; verified before deployment. SLSA Level 2 provenance (signed, timestamped, builder-attested) reachable in afternoon on GitHub Actions. Blocks tampering via cosign verify checks. For self-hosted Forgejo: manual cosign setup needed (more ops burden).
recommendedStack.piNote: Cosign runs on both platforms. GitHub Actions (keyless) on Proxmox x86 runners preferred. Forgejo: manual cosign + self-hosted Sigstore complexity. Pi can verify signatures before deployment (minimal CPU overhead).

interviewDecisionPoints.question: Will you deploy a centralized single-Proxmox-box threat detection system, or a distributed hybrid (Proxmox + Pi edge sensors)?
options: Single Proxmox x86 only (simplest ops, highest cost/power)
Proxmox x86 + Raspberry Pi 5 edge (recommended for 2026: cost-efficient, resilient, leverages Pi's low power for DNS/passive monitoring)
Multi-node Proxmox cluster (overkill unless threat-detection scales to 10+ sensors or multi-gigabit throughput)
interviewDecisionPoints.recommendation: Proxmox x86 + Raspberry Pi 5 hybrid. Pi 5 as edge DNS resolver (AdGuard Home, <5W power, always-on) + optional lightweight Suricata. Proxmox x86 as centralized SOC (Suricata + Zeek cluster + RITA + ClickHouse + Grafana). Decouples concerns (network appliance vs. analysis backend), fault-tolerant (Pi failure doesn't kill threat detection), cost-effective (<$400 total).

interviewDecisionPoints.question: What is acceptable threat-response latency between detection and automatic block?
options: Sub-millisecond (XDP kernel-level, no userspace latency): Suricata eBPF/XDP on x86 NIC (~0.2-0.5ms)
Sub-10ms (nftables dynamic sets, acceptable for home networks): add/remove rules in kernel (~100us-1ms, plus detection pipeline latency)
Sub-100ms (acceptable if human review step): API calls to pfSense/OPNsense firewall, orchestration overhead
interviewDecisionPoints.recommendation: Sub-10ms (nftables). Suricata eBPF/XDP requires Intel/Mellanox NIC (Pi unsupported, RTL8111 lacks XDP). For maximum compatibility: Proxmox nftables + Suricata EVE JSON parsing + atomic rule injection. Total pipeline latency: detection (0.1ms) + EVE parse (5ms) + nftables add (100us) = ~5.2ms acceptable for home network. If single-NIC bottleneck, fallback to sub-100ms orchestration tier (pfSense API, 2-5 second operator review gate for safety).

interviewDecisionPoints.question: Should detected threats trigger automatic blocking, or require human approval before enforcement?
options: Fully autonomous (zero-touch, auto-block high-confidence threats within 10 seconds)
Operator-gated (Suricata alert → webhook → Grafana notification → operator clicks 'Isolate' in web UI → nftables/VLAN enforcement)
Hybrid: auto-block only for specific threat patterns (e.g., known C2 C-blocks), operator-gate for anomalies
interviewDecisionPoints.recommendation: Hybrid (best practice). Auto-block high-confidence composite signals: (RITA beaconing alert AND JA4 malicious C2 fingerprint) → nftables drop within 5-10 seconds (no review). Operator-gate lower-confidence anomalies: (Isolation Forest volumetric outlier) → Grafana alert → operator reviews context (host identity, baseline) → decide block/whitelist. Prevents false-positive lockout risk while enabling emergency response on known threats.

interviewDecisionPoints.question: Should the system inspect encrypted HTTPS traffic (MITM via mitmproxy/SSLsplit) for deeper visibility, or remain payload-agnostic?
options: Payload-agnostic (passive JA3/JA4 fingerprinting + DNS logging pre-encryption, no decryption, zero privacy violation)
Selective MITM on isolated VLAN (untrusted IoT segment only, requires manual CA installation on devices)
Full MITM (all traffic, maximum visibility, breaks end-to-end encryption, regulatory+privacy risk)
interviewDecisionPoints.recommendation: Payload-agnostic primary, with optional selective MITM. JA3/JA4 encrypted traffic fingerprinting + DNS logging (pre-encryption ground truth) cover 90% of threat detection without touching encryption. Optional: SSLsplit transparent proxy on isolated IoT VLAN (smart TV, fitness tracker) for deeper DPI without family privacy concerns. Avoid full-network MITM (legally/ethically fraught even in your own home). ECH (RFC 9849) will break SNI visibility by 2026 anyway; DNS-first strategy already resilient.

interviewDecisionPoints.question: Should threat intel be sourced from free community feeds (ThreatFox, GreyNoise Community) or commercial vendors (Spamhaus, ET Pro rules)?
options: Free only (abuse.ch ThreatFox API, GreyNoise Community, ET Open rulesets)
Freemium (free tiers + optional paid subscriptions for advanced features: Spamhaus API, ET Pro ruleset ~$1000/yr)
Enterprise (premium commercial feeds: Censys, Shodan, Anomali for adversary infrastructure tracking)
interviewDecisionPoints.recommendation: Freemium. ThreatFox (free, 500+ orgs, updated daily) + GreyNoise Community (free IP reputation) + ET Open (free, community rules). Budget ~$500-1000/yr for Spamhaus paid API (domain/IP reputation) if feasible. ET Pro ruleset ($1000+/yr) nice-to-have but ET Open sufficient for home network (covers 80% of active malware families). Skip enterprise ($5K+/yr per feed); overkill for home.

interviewDecisionPoints.question: How long should threat-detection data persist for forensic analysis and trending?
options: 30 days (recent logs only, minimal storage: ClickHouse tier-1, SSD)
90-180 days (quarterly trends, moderate storage: ClickHouse + local NVMe pool)
1+ year (regulatory/personal compliance, large storage: S3 cold tier, 10x cost increase)
interviewDecisionPoints.recommendation: 90-180 days on Proxmox NVMe (primary), with automated S3 export for archival backup (optional). ClickHouse achieves 10TB/year per 100 Mbps throughput sustained (highly compressed). 90 days = ~2.5TB SSD allocation on Proxmox. This timeframe enables threat hunting (anomaly baselines shift bi-weekly), trend analysis, and forensic post-incident reviews. S3 archival (optional, $50-200/yr) for long-term compliance if needed.

interviewDecisionPoints.question: Should you build threat-detection from component tools (Suricata+Zeek+RITA+ClickHouse) or deploy ready-made appliance (SELKS 10)?
options: Build from scratch (maximum flexibility, 2-3 months setup/tuning, learning curve steep, ops burden high)
Assemble (SELKS 10 base + extend with ClickHouse/Grafana for analytics, ~2 weeks setup, moderate flexibility)
Pure appliance (SELKS 10 only, zero customization, 3 days setup, minimal ops but limited long-term analytics)
interviewDecisionPoints.recommendation: Assemble (SELKS 10 + ClickHouse/Grafana extension). SELKS 10 provides production-ready Suricata IDS/IPS + Arkime forensics out-of-box (eliminates tuning burden). Extend with ClickHouse for long-term unified analytics and Grafana for dashboard unification. Pure build adds 6-8 weeks without material capability gain (Arkime v5.0 JA4 fingerprinting is SELKS-bundled, ClickHouse integration bleeding-edge). Pure appliance misses long-term threat trending (analytics is where home-lab value accrues). Assemble: 80% time-to-value with 20% effort.

interviewDecisionPoints.question: Proxmox VE (x86-only) or alternative open-source hypervisor (KVM-only, Xen, or lightweight Docker on bare Linux)?
options: Proxmox VE 8.x (recommended, mature, web UI, clustering support, OpenTofu/Ansible ecosystem)
Bare KVM + libvirt (headless, steep CLI learning curve, no web UI)
Docker Swarm (simpler than Kubernetes, but limited scaling, no VM support for multi-OS environments)
Kubernetes k3s on Linux (universal, but overhead for threat-detection-only workload)
interviewDecisionPoints.recommendation: Proxmox VE 8.x. Mature, production-proven, superb web UI (no CLI required), OpenTofu/bpg provider enables IaC. Supports both VMs (Suricata, Zeek, Wazuh) and LXC containers (lightweight, faster startup). Clustering ready for future HA expansion. Alternative: k3s on Linux if you want pure container orchestration + GitOps (ArgoCD); adds complexity for home lab. Avoid bare KVM (CLI-heavy, no clustering, operational burden).

interviewDecisionPoints.topic: Raspberry Pi vs. Proxmox x86 Sizing
interviewDecisionPoints.question: What home network bandwidth (sustained Mbps) and device count (# of endpoints)?
options: Small: <100 Mbps, <50 devices (Pi 4/5 sufficient for all services: DNS, lightweight Suricata, passive monitoring)
Medium: 100-500 Mbps, 50-200 devices (Proxmox x86 primary, Pi 5 optional edge sensor)
Large: >500 Mbps or >200 devices (Proxmox x86 required, Pi as telemetry-only edge, multi-node clustering needed)
interviewDecisionPoints.recommendation: Assess your ISP broadband (typical home: 100-500 Mbps); device count (typical home: 30-100 devices including IoT). If <200 Mbps and <100 devices: Pi 5 standalone (combined DNS+Suricata) viable. If 200-500 Mbps: Proxmox x86 primary (Suricata 1+ Gbps capable) + Pi 5 secondary (DNS, optional ntopng passive). If >500 Mbps: Proxmox multi-core (8+ vCPU for full Zeek cluster), Pi optional telemetry. Most home networks fall in 'medium' category; recommend hybrid (Proxmox + Pi).

interviewDecisionPoints.question: Should infrastructure be IaC-provisioned (Terraform/OpenTofu) and GitOps-deployed (ArgoCD), or manually configured?
options: Full IaC/GitOps (OpenTofu + bpg/proxmox + ArgoCD + Suricata rules as Git commits, 2 weeks setup, production-grade, future-proof)
Hybrid IaC (OpenTofu for infrastructure, manual rule tuning, ~1 week setup, good for learning)
Manual (Proxmox web UI, SSH, no version control, lowest barrier to entry, technical debt accumulates)
interviewDecisionPoints.recommendation: Hybrid IaC (starting point). Use OpenTofu for Proxmox VM/LXC provisioning (version-controlled, repeatable). Configure threat-detection tools (Suricata, Zeek) via Ansible playbooks (post-provisioning). Store all rules, Ansible playbooks in Git (audit trail, rollback capability). Avoid full GitOps (ArgoCD adds complexity for home lab; reserve for team-scale deployments). This approach balances DevSecOps maturity (infrastructure auditable) with pragmatism (rule tuning remains manual until you reach >10 detection nodes).

risks: ECH (Encrypted Client Hello, RFC 9849) Adoption Blindness: By 2026, ~50% of clients will use ECH, eliminating SNI visibility from TLS handshakes. Passive threat detection relying on SNI-based rules will fail. Mitigation: Shift to DNS-first visibility strategy NOW (AdGuard Home logs pre-encryption DNS queries). JA4/JA4T encrypted traffic fingerprinting provides behavioral signal independent of SNI. Accept 50% SNI-opaque traffic; compensate with JA4 + DNS correlation.

False-Positive Killswitch Lock-Out: Aggressive automatic killswitch on anomaly-based detection can catastrophically block legitimate traffic (Windows Update, new SaaS signup, cloud backup). Device owner loses internet. Mitigation: Composite signal requirement (signature detection OR (anomaly 1 AND anomaly 2)). High-confidence thresholds (top 0.1% Isolation Forest outliers). Automatic blocks TTL-expired (5m-1h) unless operator renews.

Supply Chain Compromise of CI/CD Tools: Trivy (March 2026), Codecov, XZ Utils precedent shows OSS tools are attack targets. Malicious SCA/SAST could inject backdoors into detection rules or infrastructure code. Mitigation: Pin all GitHub Actions to commit SHAs (StepSecurity Harden-Runner auto-pins). Verify Suricata rule signatures via ET digest. Use OSV-Scanner instead of Trivy. Air-gap Git repository if possible.

Regulatory/Privacy Violation: Even in home network, encrypting DNS or capturing TLS handshakes to centralized database could trigger privacy laws (GDPR Right to Erasure, COPPA, HIPAA if health-tracking IoT). Mitigation: Ingest metadata ONLY (no payloads, no long-term IPs). DNS logs auto-expire after 90 days. TLS fingerprints (JA4) are pseudonymous. Avoid MITM unless isolated to high-risk segments. Document retention policy; inform household members.

Operational Fatigue: Alert volume from Suricata + Zeek overwhelms operator. Daily noise leads to alert fatigue → ignoring real threats. Mitigation: Aggressive alert tuning (block bottom 95% of low-confidence alerts via Suricata suppress rules). Alert only on composite signals. Use Grafana to surface only high-confidence threats (RITA high-count beacons, top 0.1% Isolation Forest flows). Weekly alert review: retire rules with >1% false positives.

Proxmox Single Point of Failure: If x86 appliance crashes, all threat detection stops. Pi can run DNS but cannot do deep DPI/IPS. Mitigation: Deploy on reliable hardware (NVMe, UPS, active cooling). Use systemd watchdog to auto-restart crashed services. Optional: 2-node Proxmox HA cluster (~$600, adds complexity). Pi as backup DNS resolver (dual DHCP). Set expectations: threat detection is defense-in-depth, not sole security control.

Raspberry Pi 4 Resource Bottleneck: Pi 4 saturates at 50-100 Mbps packet processing. Suricata rule drop > 20% at sustained 100 Mbps if CPU-bound. Mitigation: Require Pi 5 (quad-core, active cooling) for production Suricata. Pi 4 acceptable for DNS-only or very light Suricata (ET minimal ruleset, <10 rules). Test baseline: 30-day sustained traffic test, measure packet loss.

NIC Driver Support Gaps: Suricata eBPF/XDP recommended (2024-2025 bleeding-edge), but RTL8111 (Pi Ethernet, most consumer NICs) lack XDP driver hooks. Can't use XDP_DROP acceleration. Mitigation: Acknowledge: most home networks cannot use AF_XDP. Fallback to AF_PACKET fanout (battle-tested on RTL8111). Proxmox x86 with Intel NIC can leverage XDP if available (i40e, ice drivers).

Wazuh Manager Resource Overhead: Wazuh 4.12+ ARM64 support promised but manager heavyweight (3GB+ RAM, PostgreSQL). Pi 5 marginal for running full manager. Mitigation: Deploy Wazuh manager on Proxmox x86 VM (2-4 vCPU, 4GB RAM minimum). Lightweight agents on Pi 5 and endpoints for FIM/log forwarding. Proxmox as Wazuh hub, Pi as telemetry spoke.

DHCP Fingerprinting Blind Spot: Static IP devices (servers, printers, some IoT) never DHCP and thus never fingerprinted. Device inventory incomplete. Mitigation: Combine DHCP with passive p0f OS detection (TCP/IP stack signatures from live traffic). Manual whitelisting for known static devices. ARP reconciliation (arp-scan hourly) catches MAC→IP mapping for statics.

Cost Creep: Proxmox CapEx + Falco/Tetragon + Wazuh agents + ClickHouse storage + commercial ET Pro rules can exceed $2K/yr. Budget-conscious home labs abandon mid-implementation. Mitigation: Start minimal (Pi 5 + Proxmox mini-PC + free ET Open rules = $350 CapEx, <$30/yr OpEx). Delay Wazuh/Falco/ET Pro until need demonstrated. Most home labs never exceed $600 total if scoped realistically.

Kubernetes (k3s) Operational Overhead: k3s adds operational complexity (kubectl, Helm charts, ArgoCD). Home operator unfamiliar with Kubernetes becomes bottleneck. Mitigation: Defer k3s unless scaling to >5 services or multi-user. Start with Podman Quadlets (systemd-native, <5 min learning curve). Graduate to k3s only if multi-node clustering or complex service interdependencies emerge.
synthesis.buildVsAssemble: RECOMMEND ASSEMBLE (Not Pure Build, Not Pure Appliance). Deploy SELKS 10 (June 2024 Stamus Networks appliance) as the foundation on Proxmox x86. SELKS provides production-ready Suricata IDS/IPS + Arkime v5.0 forensics (JA4 fingerprinting, conditional packet capture reducing storage 10-100x) + EveBox threat-hunting UI, eliminating 4-6 weeks of Suricata rule tuning, Arkime indexing, ELK operational burden. Then EXTEND SELKS with: (1) ClickHouse (x86 VM) for unified logs/metrics/traces (10x storage compression vs. Elasticsearch, S3 tiering for 1-year retention). (2) Grafana (Proxmox VM) dashboards unified across ClickHouse + Prometheus host metrics + Loki logs. (3) Wazuh Manager (Proxmox VM) for threat intelligence orchestration and automated killswitch responses. (4) AdGuard Home (Pi 5) for DNS filtering and pre-encryption query logging (ECH blindness mitigation). (5) OpenTofu IaC (git-tracked Proxmox VMs) and Ansible for reproducible deployments. Why Not Pure Build? Building Suricata + Arkime + Zeek + ELK from scratch adds 8-12 weeks, steep learning curve (Arkime index tuning, Elasticsearch clustering, rule false-positive triage), and operational debt. SELKS pre-integrates these components (tested by Stamus); you inherit proven configs. Arkime v5.0 JA4 fingerprinting and conditional PCAP are bleeding-edge 2024 features—mature only in SELKS, not DIY. Why Not Pure Appliance? SELKS 10 alone caps at 90-day retention (Elasticsearch storage cost), provides limited long-term analytics, lacks unified ClickHouse storage for multi-signal correlation. Missing: flow-based anomaly detection (RITA beaconing), multi-year threat trending (impossible with 90-day windows), broader DevOps integration (IaC, CI/CD, SIEM). Pure appliance = tactical (immediate threat blocking) but not strategic (understanding network behavior long-term). Assemble Sweet Spot: SELKS 10 + ClickHouse/Grafana provides strategic + tactical: SELKS detects and blocks threats in <100ms (tactical). ClickHouse retains 90-365 days for anomaly baselines, threat trending, forensics (strategic). Grafana unifies IDS alerts + flow analytics + host health. Wazuh orchestrates multi-tool responses. OpenTofu + Ansible enable reproducible, audited infrastructure. Time & Cost: Setup 2-3 weeks (SELKS OVA import + ClickHouse VM provision + Grafana config) vs. 8-12 weeks build-from-scratch. CapEx: $400 (Proxmox x86 + Pi 5 hardware). OpEx: $50-100/yr (electricity, optional threat intel subscriptions) vs. $100-500/yr pure appliance (Elasticsearch storage, ET Pro). DevSecOps maturity: IaC-ready (OpenTofu reproducible), SIEM-ready (Wazuh integration), extensible (ClickHouse analytics). Verdict: ASSEMBLE is optimal for 2024-2026 home network threat detection. You gain bleeding-edge capabilities (SELKS Arkime JA4, ClickHouse unified storage, Wazuh orchestration) with mature, production-tested foundation (SELKS), while avoiding both the complexity of build-from-scratch and limitations of pure appliance.

rawFindings.domain: Home Network Traffic Monitoring, Threat Detection, and Automatic Killswitch with Kernel Datapaths (libpcap, AF_PACKET, AF_XDP, eBPF/XDP, PF_RING, DPDK)

technologies.name: libpcap + AF_PACKET (TPACKET_V3)
technologies.summary: Kernel-space ring buffer packet capture using TPACKET_V3 block-level polling. Performance ~700 Mb/s single-stream, 1.3-1.4 Gb/s with AF_PACKET fanout load-balancing across multiple CPU cores. Well-supported on all Linux distributions and ARM platforms. Industry-standard for tcpdump, Zeek, Suricata.
pros: Ubiquitous Linux support across x86 and ARM64 (including Pi 4/5)
TPACKET_V3 block-level polling reduces CPU overhead by 15-20%
AF_PACKET fanout supports HASH, LB (round-robin), CPU, RND, ROLLOVER, QM policies
Fanout distributes load equally across N sockets on N cores (optimal: PACKET_FANOUT_CPU)
Minimal packet loss even on 1Gbps links with proper CPU affinity
Works through Proxmox bridge via tc mirred + tcpdump; works on transparent Linux bridge on Pi
cons: Single-stream limited to ~700 Mb/s; fanout required for >1Gbps
Kernel memory overhead accumulates with buffer sizing
No zero-copy within userspace (packets copied from kernel ring)
Requires manual fanout configuration; default single-socket underutilizes multi-core
technologies.fitForProject: Highly recommended baseline for both Pi and Proxmox. Use AF_PACKET v3 fanout for >1Gbps capacity. Suricata and Zeek both support native fanout.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi 4/5 ARM64: achieves 100-700 Mb/s sustained with proper CPU pinning; scales to ~1Gbps with fanout on Pi 5's quad cores. Proxmox x86: full line-rate 1-2.5Gbps per interface with fanout.

technologies.name: AF_XDP (eBPF-based kernel bypass)
technologies.summary: eXpress Data Path allows eBPF programs to intercept packets at driver hooks, bypassing network stack via XDP_REDIRECT to AF_XDP sockets. Single-stream 1.3 Gb/s, scales to 186 Gb/s on 8-CPU bench with 1200-byte packets (18.8 Mpps). Packets dropped at earliest stage = minimal latency.
pros: Extreme performance: 186 Gb/s multi-stream scaling (2024 benchmarks on capable hardware)
Single-stream 1.3-1.4 Gb/s vs AF_PACKET's 700 Mb/s; 2x improvement
Bypass eliminates TCP/IP stack processing; sub-microsecond latency
Can enforce drop/redirect/modify at XDP layer for killer/killswitch decisions
Modern drivers (Intel i40e/ice, Mellanox, Broadcom) gaining native XDP support
cons: Limited NIC driver support; most consumer hardware not yet compatible
Requires Linux kernel 4.15+; optimal with 5.8+ for AF_XDP socket type
Complex development: needs clang, libbpf, eBPF bytecode maintenance
Hardware offload still experimental; software offload can saturate CPU
Steep learning curve for custom threat detection logic in eBPF
technologies.fitForProject: Emerging choice for 2025+ deployments on supported x86 hardware (Intel N100+ NICs). Avoid on Raspberry Pi 4—Pi 5 with newer ARM kernel possible but untested. Consider for Proxmox inline threat response (killswitch drops at XDP layer).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi 4: no practical AF_XDP support (driver compatibility absent). Pi 5: theoretical but unproven; modern arm64 kernel 6.1+ may support on USB NICs. Proxmox x86: full production-ready on Intel-based systems with i40e/ice NICs.

technologies.name: PF_RING ZC (Zero-Copy)
technologies.summary: High-performance ring-buffer engine supporting 100+ Gbps line rate with zero-copy on supported NICs (Intel, NVIDIA/Mellanox, Napatech, Silicom). Minimal packet loss; PF_RING 8.4+ adds zero-copy for Intel Virtual Functions (iavf-zc).
pros: Production-proven at 100+ Gbps enterprise scale
Zero-copy implementation minimizes CPU overhead and latency
Inter-process and inter-VM communication patterns for KVM sensor architectures
Hardware offload support for Mellanox, Intel, Napatech adapters
Virtual Function (VF) support enables high-speed capture from Proxmox VM passthrough
Flexible API (queue, worker, pool) for multi-threaded applications
cons: Requires Linux kernel module installation and maintenance
Most beneficial with specialized NICs; generic drivers see marginal gains
Licensing ambiguity; ZC module may have restrictions on certain hardware
ARM (Raspberry Pi) support undocumented and likely absent
Overkill for sub-10Gbps home networks
technologies.fitForProject: Not recommended for this home network use case. Complexity/overkill for 100Mbps-2.5Gbps throughput. Reserved for enterprise 10Gbps+ networks or Proxmox setups with dedicated Mellanox SmartNICs.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: No support. Proxmox x86: Viable only with enterprise NIC investment; diminishing returns below 10Gbps.

technologies.name: DPDK (Data Plane Development Kit)
technologies.summary: Intel-led framework providing Poll Mode Drivers (PMDs) for userspace NIC access, bypassing kernel completely. Achieves 10-100 Mpps per core (vs 1-2 Mpps kernel). DPDK 24.11 released with new drivers (Cisco ENIC, Marvell CN20K, Realtek, ZTE) and logging enhancements.
pros: Extreme packet-processing rates: 10-100 Mpps per core on modern hardware
Eliminates kernel network stack entirely; predictable low latency
Broad NIC support; new drivers added quarterly (DPDK 24.11, 25.03 coming)
AF_XDP integration allows eBPF -> userspace hand-off without full bypass
Widely used in NFV, DPI, packet generation (pktgen-dpdk)
Multi-queue awareness; CPU affinity built-in
cons: Massive complexity; requires custom C/Rust application development
Monopolizes NIC descriptor queues; no standard packet capture tools (tcpdump incompatible)
Requires HugePages memory allocation; OS management overhead
No practical ARM support; DPDK barely tested on Pi
Overkill for rule-based IDS/threat detection; better for custom NDR/DPI pipelines
technologies.fitForProject: Not recommended for home network. Suited only for custom DPI/NDR appliance development. For managed IDS (Suricata, Zeek), AF_PACKET fanout is superior.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: Completely unsupported. Proxmox x86: Production-viable only for custom packet-processing appliances, not standard threat detection.

technologies.name: eBPF/XDP with Suricata
technologies.summary: Suricata 7.0+ integrates native eBPF/XDP offload, allowing rule evaluation at driver hook layer before kernel stack. Packets dropped at XDP layer if matched. Requires Linux 4.13+, clang, libbpf. Enables automatic killswitch via XDP_DROP action.
pros: Native IDS rules compiled to eBPF bytecode; rule evaluation at line rate
XDP_DROP enforcement allows killswitch without inline proxy overhead
Bypass: packets dropped at earliest stage (before IP reassembly, TCP buffering)
Sub-microsecond latency for threat-triggered drops
Suricata 7.0+ officially supports eBPF/XDP offload configuration
Cilium Tetragon adds policy-based enforcement with <1% overhead
cons: Kernel 4.15+ required; ARM64 support nascent (Suricata docs warn of NIC compatibility gaps)
Encrypted (TLS 443) traffic creates blind spots; no deep packet inspection
CPU requirements on 64+ core systems need manual tuning
VLAN tracking must align between eBPF code and Suricata config
eBPF flow map persistence issues; cleanup required before filter reload
Hardware NIC offload still experimental; most deployments use software XDP
technologies.fitForProject: Excellent for 2025+ Proxmox x86 deployments. Use for automatic killswitch on detected threats. Avoid on Pi 4; Pi 5 possible if kernel 6.1+ with compatible driver.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi 4: Not practical (driver support absent, CPU-intensive software XDP not worth overhead). Pi 5: Theoretical with recent kernel + Suricata 7.0, but unproven; recommend AF_PACKET fanout baseline. Proxmox x86: Production-ready; use with Suricata 7.0+ for killswitch automation.

technologies.name: Netmap (userspace NIC abstraction)
technologies.summary: Fast userspace packet I/O via memory-mapped buffers. Supports multiple drivers (Intel, Broadcom, Realtek). Integrates with libpcap via pcap-netmap backend. Enables Mpps-scale processing without kernel overhead.
pros: Ultra-fast ring buffers; 14.8 Mpps per core reported
Seamless libpcap integration (tcpdump over netmap supported)
Support for generic drivers via emulation layer (slow emulation mode)
Zero-copy between userspace and NIC
cons: Limited modern driver support; newer hardware often unsupported
Requires kernel module; less actively maintained than DPDK
No ARM porting effort evident
Licensing/maintenance unclear; superseded by AF_XDP in recent years
technologies.fitForProject: Legacy option. AF_PACKET fanout is simpler and better maintained. Consider only if you have legacy Netmap-aware tools.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: No support. Proxmox x86: Viable for legacy setups, but AF_PACKET/AF_XDP preferred.

technologies.name: Managed Switch SPAN/Port Mirror (Hardware)
technologies.summary: Layer 2 switch feature (SPAN = Switched Port Analyzer) duplicating traffic from source port(s) to monitor port. Configuration via CLI (Cisco, TP-Link, NETGEAR). Copies RX/TX to single destination port (receive-only).
pros: Zero CPU/software overhead; pure hardware switching
Captures all traffic including Layer 1 errors, malformed frames
Simple to configure on managed L2/L3 switches
Non-intrusive; doesn't affect monitored links
Supports Local SPAN (single switch), RSPAN (VLAN tunnel), ERSPAN (GRE tunnel)
cons: SPAN destination port is receive-only; cannot inject return traffic
Switch prioritizes real-time traffic over SPAN; drops SPAN copies under load
Filtered packets (undersized, errors) don't reach SPAN port
Only captures external traffic; misses east-west traffic between local VMs/containers
Requires managed switch; not available on consumer unmanaged switches
technologies.fitForProject: Recommended as primary tap for external WAN/LAN traffic. Wire switch SPAN -> sensor network interface (Pi or Proxmox). Pair with Linux bridge tc mirred for internal VM-to-VM capture.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Hardware-agnostic. Both Pi and Proxmox can receive SPAN traffic equally well. For home network: place Pi on SPAN port for lightweight capture; or Proxmox x86 for VM-based Suricata/Zeek.

technologies.name: Linux Transparent Bridge + tc mirred (Software)
technologies.summary: Software-based traffic mirroring via Linux tc (traffic control) mirred action. Create bridge, attach interfaces, set ingress/egress qdisc filters to mirror packets to dummy/veth interface. No hardware SPAN required. Works on any Linux host (Pi, Proxmox LXC/VM).
pros: Zero hardware cost; software-only on any Linux kernel (2.6.38+)
Flexible: mirror ingress, egress, or both; per-protocol filtering
Integrates with Linux bridge (br_netfilter) for L2 transparency
Enables east-west traffic capture (VM-to-VM, container-to-container)
Combined with ebtables/iptables for Layer 2/3 filtering upstream
cons: CPU overhead; processing duplicate packets consumes cycles
Configuration not persistent across reboot (crontab required)
Must enable promiscuous mode on tap interface to see non-broadcast
One direction of traffic (RX or TX) sometimes missing without careful qdisc setup
Requires deep iptables/tc knowledge; error-prone configuration
technologies.fitForProject: Essential for Proxmox: mirror VM traffic within virtual switch to sensor VM. Use for internal network segmentation monitoring. On Pi: use if deploying as transparent bridge between WAN and LAN.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: Viable; tc runs on ARM64. CPU overhead manageable up to 1Gbps if bridge is passthrough-only (no heavy filtering). Proxmox: Standard practice; OVS/Linux bridge mirror well-documented; tc performance adequate for 10Gbps on x86.

technologies.name: Raspberry Pi Transparent Bridge (ebtables + br_netfilter)
technologies.summary: Configure Pi as Layer 2 transparent bridge between WAN (eth0) and LAN (USB eth1 or second NIC). Use ebtables for L2 filtering, iptables for L3 filtering through bridge-netfilter. Captures all bridged traffic.
pros: Zero IP configuration; bridge is transparent to DHCP/routing
ebtables filters traffic at bridge-netfilter layer before IP stack
Low cost (~$5 USB NIC adds second port to Pi 4; Pi 5 has PCIe for NVMe or NIC card)
Minimal power draw (idle ~2-3W, active ~5-10W)
Ideal form factor for edge placement near router/modem
Supports both single-port mirroring and full bidirectional bridge
cons: Pi 4 has single Gigabit NIC; requires USB Ethernet adapter for second port (reduced throughput)
Pi 5 PCIe 2.0 x1 supports NVMe but not additional NIC (must use USB); USB 3.0 to GigE viable
Thermal dissipation at sustained 1Gbps requires heatsink/cooling
Single Cortex-A72 (Pi 4) / A76 (Pi 5) CPU core handling interrupts becomes bottleneck >800Mbps
ebtables rules complex; requires bridge-netfilter kernel module (modprobe br_netfilter)
br_netfilter must be loaded; unavailable in some stripped kernels
technologies.fitForProject: Highly recommended for this project. Deploy Pi as inline transparent bridge between router and LAN switch/modem. Capture with tcpdump on dummy interface. Run Suricata in lightweight AF_PACKET fanout mode. Cost-effective, low power.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: Sweet spot for transparent bridge appliance. Low CapEx, low OpEx, always-on (5-10W). Proxmox: Overkill; x86 idle power 30-50W. Use Proxmox for centralized VM-based sensors + analysis, Pi for distributed edge tap.

technologies.name: Proxmox Linux Bridge + OVS Port Mirror
technologies.summary: Proxmox x86 hosts VMs/LXCs via Linux bridge or OpenVSwitch. Attach physical SPAN interface to Proxmox bridge. Use ovs-vsctl to configure mirror: source port = all, destination = sensor VM tap interface. Sensor VM runs Suricata/Zeek on captured traffic.
pros: Enterprise-grade hypervisor; full Kubernetes/cloud-native support
OVS mirrors support both local and remote VLAN-based RSPAN
Unlimited VM/LXC scaling for multi-sensor architectures
x86 native support for DPDK, PF_RING, full Suricata/Zeek ruleset
High availability clustering for redundant sensors
Persistent storage; sensor state survives reboots
cons: OVS mirror config NOT persistent; requires crontab restoration post-reboot
Tap device naming (tapVMIDi0) must match sensor VM; error-prone manual setup
Bidirectional traffic capture requires careful ingress/egress qdisc mirroring
High idle power (30-50W for N100 mini-PC baseline)
Licensing; Proxmox VE free but commercial support recommended
Storage overhead: sensor VMs/LXCs require SSD; 16GB+ RAM ideal
technologies.fitForProject: Recommended for centralized threat detection architecture. Deploy Proxmox 8+ with 2-3 sensor VMs (Suricata, Zeek, Wazuh) capturing from SPAN mirror. Use LXC containers for lightweight agents.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox: Production-grade; scales to 10+ sensors. Pi: Cannot run Proxmox in production (ARM community port unstable for sensors). Use Pi for edge bridge, Proxmox for centralized SOC.

technologies.name: Suricata 7.0+ with Fanout + Threat Rules
technologies.summary: Production IDS engine supporting AF_PACKET fanout, eBPF/XDP, threaded processing. Evaluates 70,000+ ET Pro rules per packet at ~700 Mb/s (AF_PACKET fanout) to 1+ Gbps (eBPF/XDP). Outputs JSON alerts, metrics, and kan trigger automated response.
pros: Active development; v7.0+ released Feb 2025 with native eBPF support
ET Pro ruleset (Emerging Threats) = 70K+ rules for malware, exploits, C&C, botnets
Multi-threaded fanout; saturates Pi 4 at ~100-200 Mbps, Proxmox at 1-2 Gbps
JSON output integrates with Wazuh, ELK, Splunk
Auto-response (flow drop, block) via XDP_DROP or nfqueue
ARM64 builds available; Raspberry Pi 5 16GB achieves 100-150 Mbps sustained
Zeek integration via Corelight feeds for correlated detection
cons: Full ruleset (70K rules) causes 20-30% packet drop at >100 Mbps on Pi 4
Requires CPU pinning and fanout tuning for >500 Mbps sustained
ET Pro ruleset paid subscription (~$1000/yr for org); free ET Open available
False positive rate 50-80% out-of-box; heavy rule tuning required
Encrypted (TLS 443) traffic invisible; no DPI on HTTPS
technologies.fitForProject: Essential component. Deploy on Proxmox for centralilzed detection (1-2 Gbps capacity). Or on Pi for edge detection (100 Mbps, rule subset). Use ET Pro ruleset + custom threat rules for killswitch automation.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi 4: ~100 Mbps sustained, light rule tuning, 2 CPU cores dedicated. Pi 5: ~200-300 Mbps sustained, 4 cores. Proxmox x86: 1+ Gbps full ruleset, unlimited cores.

technologies.name: Zeek (Bro) with AF_PACKET Plugin
technologies.summary: Flow-based NDR (Network Detection and Response) tool. Captures network metadata (IPs, ports, protocols, TLS certs, HTTP URIs, DNS queries). Zeek AF_PACKET plugin supports fanout. Lighter CPU than Suricata; focuses on anomaly detection, not signatures.
pros: Light CPU overhead; 50-100 Mbps per core on Pi 5, 500+ Mbps per core on x86
Excellent for IoT/smart home monitoring (identifies anomalous DNS, SSH, port scans)
Outputs CSV/JSON for correlation with Suricata alerts
Rich scripting language (ZeekLang) for custom detection rules
Zeek AF_PACKET plugin (GitHub: zeek/zeek-af_packet-plugin) mature
Synergistic with Suricata: Zeek telemetry + Suricata IDS = defense-in-depth
cons: No signature-based threat blocking (detection only; no auto-response)
Metadata capture misses encrypted payload analysis
Scripting steep learning curve; default scripts may not suit home networks
Less frequent updates than Suricata; community-driven
technologies.fitForProject: Recommended as secondary detection layer. Pair Zeek (on Pi or lightweight LXC) with Suricata for complementary detection. Zeek's DNS/TLS logging ideal for identifying C&C, phishing.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi 4: ~50 Mbps sustained. Pi 5: ~100-150 Mbps sustained. Proxmox x86: 500+ Mbps per core, scales horizontally.

technologies.name: Falco + Tetragon (eBPF Runtime Security)
technologies.summary: Falco: rule-based detection of abnormal process behavior (privilege escalation, container escape, cryptomining). Tetragon: fine-grained eBPF hooks + policy enforcement (can block processes, syscalls). Both use eBPF; sub-1% CPU overhead.
pros: eBPF-based; kernel-level visibility into process, network, file syscalls
Falco v2026 now CNCF mature; Tetragon matured in 2024 v1.2
Tetragon 1.2+ excels at container escape + cryptomining detection
CPU overhead <1% for runtime security (vs 20-30% for signature IDS)
Enforcement possible: block syscalls, kill process, prevent network access
Complements Suricata for defense-in-depth: host-level + network-level threats
cons: Falco: detection-only; high false positive rate (50-80% default rules)
Tetragon: enforcement requires strict policy tuning to avoid breaking apps
Not suitable for network threat detection alone (requires app context)
Overkill for home IoT; designed for container/K8s security
technologies.fitForProject: Optional but recommended for advanced setups. Deploy on Proxmox hypervisor (kernel-level) or on sensor VMs to detect compromised Suricata/Zeek processes. Use for insider threat detection on host.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: Possible on Pi 5 with recent kernel 6.1+, but limited use case (no containers). Proxmox: Ideal for detecting rogue sensor VMs or kernel exploitation.

technologies.name: Wazuh 4.12+ (SIEM + Threat Intelligence)
technologies.summary: Open-source XDR/SIEM platform. Wazuh agents deployed on endpoints (VMs, IoT); centralizes Suricata alerts, OS logs, file integrity, vulnerability scanning. New May 2025: ARM64 core + eBPF file integrity + CTI-enriched CVE metadata.
pros: Wazuh 4.12+ (May 2025) adds ARM64 support for manager, indexer, dashboard
Integrates Suricata JSON alerts into SIEM pipeline
eBPF-based FIM (file integrity monitoring) on Linux; lightweight
CTI enrichment: CISA CVE data replaces NVD for real-world threat prioritization
Automated response rules (e.g., block user, isolate VM, trigger alert)
AI/ML threat hunting: Random Forest + DBSCAN anomaly detection
Opensearch/Elasticsearch backend for unlimited log retention
cons: Heavy resource requirements: 2GB+ RAM (manager), 4GB+ (indexer); not Pi-friendly for central server
Agent architecture requires network connectivity; agents must reach manager
Complexity: requires Elasticsearch, Kibana, or Opensearch; maintenance overhead
Steep learning curve for response automation rules (Ansible required)
technologies.fitForProject: Highly recommended as orchestration layer. Deploy Wazuh manager on Proxmox VM. Deploy lightweight agents on Pi edge sensors + VM sensors. Centralizes all threat intel; automates killswitch triggers.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: Cannot host Wazuh manager (too heavy). Can run lightweight Wazuh agent for host monitoring. Proxmox: Perfect for centralized Wazuh manager + indexer; orchestrates all sensors.

technologies.name: Cilium eBPF Dataplane (Advanced)
technologies.summary: Modern eBPF-based network policy engine replacing traditional iptables. Cilium enforces Layer 3/4/7 network policies (e.g., Pod A -> DB on port 5432 only). Hubble observability tool logs every flow. Typical overhead <1%.
pros: eBPF-based; eliminates iptables chain traversal (huge performance gain)
Layer 7 policy support (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka) not possible with iptables
Hubble flow logging enables forensics, threat correlation
Meshwide security model: default-deny everything, whitelist allowed flows
Cilium Tetragon policy enforcement (block, log, audit)
cons: Kubernetes-specific; minimal benefit for non-K8s home networks
Overkill complexity for home network
Requires kernel 5.8+ with BPF_PROG_TYPE_SOCK_OPS support
technologies.fitForProject: Not recommended for home network. Applicable only if deploying K8s cluster on Proxmox for multi-tenant threat detection.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: Impractical. Proxmox K8s: Consider for advanced multi-tenant sensor orchestration.

bleedingEdge: Suricata 7.0+ eBPF/XDP native integration (Feb 2025) enabling XDP_DROP-based killswitch auto-response without inline proxy overhead
Wazuh 4.12.0 ARM64 core architecture support (May 2025) + eBPF file integrity monitoring enabling edge manager deployment on Proxmox ARM clusters
DPDK 24.11 (Nov 2024) + AF_XDP polling mode driver integration enabling 186 Gb/s multi-stream scaling on x86 appliances
Cilium Tetragon 1.2+ (2024) with improved policy language + container escape detection outperforming Falco on cryptomining threats
Linux kernel 6.6+ XDP multi-buffer support (2024) enabling jumbo frame / segmented packet handling at driver layer
AF_PACKET fanout PACKET_FANOUT_QM queue-mapping policy (kernel 5.9+) enabling 20-30% CPU reduction via NIC RSS alignment
Proxmox 8.0+ OVS vxlan SPAN mirroring (Oct 2024) enabling remote sensor tunneling across WAN
Tetragon policy-as-code (2025) + OPA/Rego for declarative threat response automation replacing shell scripts
eBPF Ecosystem Progress 2024-2025: runtime security (Falco, Tetragon) maturation + hardware offload adoption on modern NICs
rawFindings.recommendation:
Deploy a **hybrid two-tier architecture**:

**Tier 1 (Edge Tap): Raspberry Pi 5 as Transparent Bridge**
- Wire Pi 5 (with USB 3.0 GigE NIC) between router and home network as transparent L2 bridge
- Enable ebtables + tc mirred to capture all WAN/LAN traffic to dummy interface
- Run Suricata 7.0+ with AF_PACKET fanout (2-4 threads) on light ET Open ruleset: achieves 200-300 Mbps sustained capture
- Run Zeek AF_PACKET plugin in parallel for DNS/TLS/flow telemetry
- Output JSON to Wazuh agent on Pi (lightweight endpoint monitor)
- Cost: $100-120 (Pi 5 8GB + USB NIC + heatsink + 64GB SD)
- Power: 5-10W idle, 12-15W sustained

**Tier 2 (Central Analysis): Proxmox x86 Mini-PC (Intel N100 or N200)**
- Deploy Proxmox 8.0 on Intel N100 mini-PC (16GB RAM, 256GB NVMe SSD)
- Create 3 LXC containers:
  1. **Suricata VM**: Full ET Pro ruleset, AF_PACKET fanout 4-8 threads, captures 1-2 Gbps for internal traffic mirrors + backup WAN capture
  2. **Zeek VM**: Metadata correlator, identifies anomalous DNS/C&C/exfil patterns
  3. **Wazuh Manager (v4.12+)**: Centralized SIEM, ingests alerts from both Pi and Proxmox sensors, orchestrates auto-response
- Configure Proxmox Linux bridge + tc mirred to capture inter-VM east-west traffic
- Optional: Deploy Falco/Tetragon on Proxmox kernel for runtime security (detect compromised sensors)
- Cost: $200-250 (N100 mini-PC) + $200 (NVMe SSD)
- Power: 15-25W idle, 40-50W sustained

**Killswitch Automation**:
- Use Suricata 7.0 eBPF/XDP mode on Proxmox: detected threats trigger XDP_DROP (kernel layer) without userspace proxy
- Wazuh response rule: high-confidence threat (e.g., known C&C DNS) → block IP via iptables/nftables rule on Pi bridge
- Alternative: TPROXY transparent proxy with automatic block list updated by Wazuh

**DevSecOps Story**:
- CI/CD: Store Suricata rules, Zeek scripts, Wazuh response configs in Git
- Automation: Ansible playbooks for Pi bridge setup (ebtables, tc, tcpdump), Proxmox LXC provisioning, Wazuh agent deployment
- Monitoring: Hubble-style flow logging (via Zeek/Suricata JSON) into Wazuh for full network observability
- Testing: Dalton (GitHub: secureworks/dalton) for rule validation in CI/CD pipeline

**Key Rationale**:
- Pi 5 as edge tap (cost-effective, low power, transparent bridge paradigm)
- Proxmox x86 as SOC (scalability, VM clustering, Kubernetes-ready for future multi-tenant sensors)
- AF_PACKET fanout baseline (proven, no driver issues on both ARM/x86)
- Suricata 7.0 eBPF/XDP for 2025+ killswitch (native kernel integration, no proxy latency)
- Wazuh 4.12+ ARM64 support enables Pi-hosted manager for future deployments
- Avoid: DPDK (overkill), PF_RING ZC (licensing gray area), netmap (legacy)
openQuestions: What is the home network topology? (single router + 1 LAN switch vs multiple subnets/VLANs?) Affects SPAN placement strategy.
Does the managed home switch support SPAN/port mirroring? (most consumer managed L2 switches do; verify model.) If not, Pi transparent bridge becomes mandatory.
What is the WAN throughput? (100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, 2.5 Gbps fiber?) Determines sensor tier (Pi vs Proxmox vs both).
Are x86 mini-PCs available in region/budget? (N100 vs N200 vs Ryzen 5 cost/availability affects Proxmox deployment).
Will the sensor network be isolated from production LAN? (air-gapped analysis VM vs inline bridge affects threat response latency and false positive tolerance).
Is real-time threat response required (killswitch <1ms) or post-incident forensics acceptable (hours)? Drives eBPF/XDP vs traditional IPS decision.
Do you need container orchestration (K8s via Proxmox)? Justifies Cilium eBPF policy engine; otherwise overkill.
What endpoint OS diversity? (Windows, Linux, macOS, IoT) affects Wazuh agent deployment complexity and threat detection ruleset choice.
Is open-source only acceptable or is commercial ET Pro ruleset budget available? (ET Pro $1000+/yr accelerates threat detection but requires licensing review).
