technologies.name: Suricata 7.x (current stable) / 9.x (dev)
technologies.summary: Multi-threaded IDS/IPS with AF_PACKET/XDP capture modes. Outputs EVE JSON (structured alerts/metadata). AF_XDP via eBPF enables zero-copy packet delivery; XDP_DRV preferred for best performance. Suricata 7.0+ resolves VirtIO NIC stability in IPS mode (critical for Proxmox VMs). EVE JSON pipelines enable Python-driven automation for conditional killswitch triggers.
pros: Native multithreading; faster threat detection than Zeek (800 Mbps - 1 Gbps per core)
AF_XDP zero-copy on compatible NICs eliminates kernel overhead; Busy-Polling (SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, Linux 5.11+) reduces latency
EVE JSON output (standardized, machine-readable); integrates directly with Python automation frameworks for auto-killswitch
Active IPS mode (not passive); can drop/reject at packet level
Raspberry Pi 5 with USB3 GigE adapter viable for light monitoring (<100 Mbps sustained)
cons: Lighter protocol metadata than Zeek; signature-dependent (requires rule updates)
Proxmox deployment: AF_PACKET/XDP requires Linux kernel 5.11+, driver support varies (some virtio drivers had instability pre-7.0)
Pi 4 single-core perf ~100-150 Mbps (thermal throttle risk without cooling); Pi 5 ~250-400 Mbps with aggressive tuning
Memory overhead on Pi: ~100-200 MB base + rule-dependent growth
technologies.fitForProject: PRIMARY for Proxmox x86 (full performance, EVE JSON automation-ready). SECONDARY for Pi (viable only if <100 Mbps monitoring, heavy rule filtering needed)
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox: 60 Gbps+ with hardware NIC + 16+ cores. Pi: ~400 Mbps ceiling (Pi 5 with tuning, ~100 Mbps sustained under thermal load). Proxmox enables multi-core scaling + VM isolation; Pi requires single instance with simplified rulesets.

technologies.name: Zeek (formerly Bro)
technologies.summary: Event-driven network analysis framework (not traditional IDS). Generates 70+ log types, 3000+ trackable events. Deep stateful protocol parsing (DNS, HTTP, SSL/TLS, SMB, etc.). Structured logs enable threat hunting and forensic analysis. 2024-2025: integrated SIEM workflows, reduced false positives via ML context.
pros: Per-device 'who-talks-to-whom' visibility at application layer; protocol-agnostic (decryption-aware for TLS metadata)
70+ structured log types; integrates seamlessly with SIEM (Elasticsearch, Splunk) for correlation
Event-driven scripting model enables custom detection policies (Zeek script language)
Minimal signature maintenance vs Suricata (relies on protocol semantics)
Forensic gold standard: 2025 research shows 91% threat detection accuracy + 7% false positives when paired with SIEM
cons: PASSIVE ONLY (no active threat response); requires paired IDS (Suricata) for blocking
Resource-intensive: 1 core handles 800 Mbps - 1 Gbps; 64 GB RAM minimum for 100+ Mbps; 128 GB for 1 Gbps
Pi 4/5 unsuitable: cluster architecture requires manager + 1+ workers; single-instance Pi <50 Mbps practical limit
Stateful connection tracking consumes RAM rapidly (6 GB per worker typical); long-lived connections spike overhead
technologies.fitForProject: PRIMARY for Proxmox x86 as contextual layer (pair with Suricata for active blocking). NOT viable for Pi (resource wall).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox: 12+ core cluster with manager (2-4 core) + workers (2 core per 100 Mbps) recommended; enables multi-Gbps analysis. Pi: Rejected (requires 64+ GB RAM minimum; Pi has 2-8 GB).

technologies.name: nDPI + ntopng
technologies.summary: ntop-maintained DPI toolkit detecting 450+ Layer-7 protocols + 56+ cybersecurity flow risks. nDPI optimized for flow monitoring (unnecessary features stripped for speed). ntopng provides web UI for real-time flows, sFlow/NetFlow/IPFIX collection. 2024: supports encrypted traffic analysis (ETA) for TLS classification without decryption.
pros: Lightweight nDPI library; runs on Linux, FreeBSD, Windows, Raspbian, x86, ARM, MIPS
450+ protocol detection (Skype, BitTorrent, P2P regardless of port obfuscation)
Flow-based analysis; ntopng dashboard shows per-host/app bandwidth allocation in real-time
Encrypted Traffic Analysis (ETA) classifies TLS/encrypted traffic without keys
Pi-friendly: ntopng community edition viable on Pi 4 (minimal overhead, UI responsive)
cons: Flow-based only; lacks packet-level inspection granularity (Suricata/Zeek provide deeper context)
ntopng web UI can be CPU-intensive with 1000+ concurrent flows; Pi CPU capped at ~80% in production
Community edition licensing limits; commercial features (advanced GeoIP, DDoS detection) require paid license
No native threat alerting/automation (UI-driven; requires external integration for killswitch)
Metadata extraction lighter than Zeek; no file transfer logging or SMB analysis
technologies.fitForProject: SECONDARY for Proxmox (complements Suricata/Zeek for flow visibility). PRIMARY for Pi (only viable DPI option for real-time dashboards without Proxmox backend).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox: scales to multi-Gbps with nProbe/nProbe Cento probes + Elasticsearch backend. Pi: ~400-500 Mbps sustainable on Pi 5 with optimized nDPI rules, <100 Mbps on Pi 4. Dashboarding practical on Pi; alerting requires external hook (webhook to firewall).

technologies.name: Arkime (formerly Moloch)
technologies.summary: Large-scale PCAP storage, indexing, and search system. Captures all packets, parses to SPI (session profile info), indexes in OpenSearch/Elasticsearch. Arkime 5 (2025): S3/HTTPS PCAP import, Cont3xt bulk enrichment, JA4 TLS fingerprinting. Designed for forensic deep-dives post-incident.
pros: 100% packet capture + Google-like search; forensic gold standard for incident investigation
Arkime 5 innovation: direct S3/HTTPS PCAP ingest (multi-region archival feasible)
JA4 TLS fingerprinting enables anomalous certificate/cipher detection
Cluster-scalable to hundreds of Gbps (storage + compute separated)
Integration with VirusTotal, Shodan, PassiveTotal for IOC enrichment
cons: Storage-intensive: 100+ Mbps uncompressed = ~50 GB/day minimum (1 year = 18 TB); Proxmox disk overhead significant
Computationally expensive: PCAP parsing + Elasticsearch indexing requires dedicated hardware; Pi unsuitable
High latency: post-hoc forensics, NOT real-time alerting (paired tool required for active response)
Operational overhead: cluster management (Parliament), index rotation, retention policies
License complexity: open-source but commercial support/SLA options from Arkime Inc.
technologies.fitForProject: OPTIONAL for Proxmox x86 (forensic layer only; requires dedicated NAS/SSD pool + ES cluster). NOT for Pi.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox only: requires 2-4 dedicated capture VMs (20-30 GB disk/day per 100 Mbps) + 1-2 ES data nodes + Parliament manager. Pi: physically impossible (1-2 TB storage, ES overhead).

technologies.name: GoFlow2 (Go NetFlow/IPFIX/sFlow Collector)
technologies.summary: High-performance NetFlow v5/v9, IPFIX, sFlow v5 collector written in Go. Modular pipeline: decode → produce (protobuf/JSON) → transport (Kafka/stdout). Horizontal scalability via Kafka; optional GeoIP/ASN enrichment. 2024: support for NATS JetStream for stream processing.
pros: Lightweight binary (Go single-file deployment); Docker-ready
Modular architecture: swap Kafka for RabbitMQ, protobuf for Avro without code changes
Parallel socket support (multiple sFlow/IPFIX listeners via URI config)
Protobuf output optimized for high-volume flows (binary efficiency)
NATS JetStream integration enables real-time stream processing + CEP (complex event processing) for threat triggers
cons: Requires flow exporter on edge devices (router/firewall must support NetFlow/IPFIX/sFlow)
No deep packet inspection; flow metadata only (source/dest IP, port, protocol, bytes, packets)
Requires external correlation logic for threat detection (not built-in)
Kafka/NATS dependency adds operational complexity (cluster management)
technologies.fitForProject: SECONDARY aggregation layer. Viable on Proxmox for flow ingest from edge exporters (softflowd on Pi-based router). NOT suitable as standalone threat detection.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox: GoFlow2 collector VM (2-4 core, 2 GB RAM) can handle 10k+ flows/sec from distributed Pi exporters. Pi: As exporter only (softflowd + GoBGP); collection must run on Proxmox backend.

technologies.name: Softflowd (NetFlow v1/5/9 Exporter)
technologies.summary: Minimal-overhead NetFlow software probe. Listens on promiscuous interface, tracks flows, exports v1/5/9 (IPv6 via v9). ~10 MB memory footprint. 2024: still widely packaged (apt install softflowd on Debian/Raspbian), stable, unmaintained upstream but battle-tested.
pros: Negligible CPU/memory overhead on Pi (5-10% single-core, <15 MB RAM)
NetFlow v9 supports IPv6 and custom fields
Works on any Linux with promiscuous NIC or TAP interface
Pairs perfectly with GoFlow2/nfdump on Proxmox backend
No kernel dependencies (pure userspace); runs on Pi OS without modification
cons: Flow sampling only; no packet payload inspection (DPI requires Suricata/nDPI upstream)
No active threat response (collector-side logic required)
Community maintenance only; no formal support
Flow template negotiation can drop packets on network congestion
technologies.fitForProject: PRIMARY exporter for Pi-based router monitoring. Deploy on Pi 4/5 sending to Proxmox GoFlow2 collector + threat correlation engine.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: Softflowd + router OS (OpenWrt/OPNsense) on Pi 4/5 = flow export at minimal overhead. Proxmox: Unnecessary (Suricata/Zeek capture natively). Combined: Pi softflowd → Proxmox GoFlow2 → SIEM/automation.

technologies.name: nfdump + nfsen (NetFlow Post-Processing + Visualization)
technologies.summary: nfdump: CLI tool for filtering/aggregating NFv5/v9/IPFIX/sFlow binary files. nfsen: RRDtool-based frontend (deprecated but stable). Modern alternative: Elasticsearch + Kibana. 2024: nfdump remains de facto standard for flow data forensics; nfsen Web UI dated but functional.
pros: nfdump CLI powerful: 'nfdump -M /data:profile -r nfcapd.* "src 192.168.1.0/24" | sort -rn | head' extracts insights instantly
Binary storage efficient: 1 year NetFlow = ~50 GB (vs Arkime PCAP ~18 TB)
Works offline; portable across systems
Pi-friendly for lightweight flow archival and queries
Integration: nfdump output → custom Python scripts for threat correlation
cons: nfsen Web UI outdated (Perl/CGI); slow with 1000+ flows/sec
No real-time alerting; batch-oriented
CLI-first UX; not suitable for NOC dashboards (requires Kibana or custom viz)
Manual profile/data retention management
technologies.fitForProject: SECONDARY for forensic flow review + long-term archival. Pair with Elasticsearch/Kibana on Proxmox for modern dashboards.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: nfdump binary storage + CLI analysis viable; archival on Pi4 with USB SSD (~1-2 years at 100 Mbps). Proxmox: nfdump + Elasticsearch for searchable historical flows; Kibana dashboards for SOC visibility.

technologies.name: Netify DPI Engine (Open-source Agent)
technologies.summary: Standalone DPI engine (built on nDPI) for gateways/firewalls. Detects 190+ protocols (file-sharing, streaming, P2P) + flow actions plugin (firewall/QoS policies). Supports x86, ARM, MIPS, PowerPC. 2024: Device Discovery plugin for IoT inventory. Open-source (netifyd) on GitHub + commercial (Netify) variants.
pros: Lightweight ARM support (optimized for OpenWrt edge routers)
190+ protocol detection with flow-level actions (drop/mark/QoS)
Device Discovery plugin identifies IoT/network assets automatically
Open-source (netifyd) on GitHub with active community (OpenWrt, OpenNSense)
Minimal overhead: viable on Pi-based firewall/router
cons: Less protocol depth than ntopng (190 vs 450+ protocols)
Flow actions require firewall integration (iptables/nftables rules)
Device Discovery requires network enumeration (ARP/mDNS scans); overhead ~5% CPU
Documentation limited; community-driven vs vendor-backed (ntopng)
technologies.fitForProject: PRIMARY for Pi-based firewall/router DPI (OpenWrt/OPNsense). Light threat detection, not full IDS replacement.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: Netify agent on OpenWrt/OPNsense firewall OS; integrates with iptables killswitch directly. Proxmox: Unnecessary (Suricata/Zeek handle DPI; Netify better at edge).

technologies.name: pmacct (Multi-purpose Flow Analyzer + NetFlow/IPFIX Exporter)
technologies.summary: Passive network monitoring toolkit supporting NetFlow, IPFIX, sFlow, libpcap, BGP, BMP, Streaming Telemetry. Version 1.7.9 (Aug 2024) release. nfacctd daemon collects flows; nfprobe exports IPFIX/NetFlow. Configurable aggregation (src/dst IP, port, protocol, TOS). Kafka plugin for streaming.
pros: Multi-protocol input: NetFlow/IPFIX/sFlow/libpcap in single daemon
IPFIX via PEN (Private Enterprise Number); vendor-neutral
Flexible aggregation: tag primitives for custom bucketing
nfprobe plugin exports IPFIX to remote collectors (GeoIP, traffic breakdown)
Kafka integration enables real-time stream processing + CEP triggers
cons: Configuration-dense (40+ knobs); steep learning curve vs simpler tools
Documentation scattered (PDF, GitHub, mailing list); not beginner-friendly
libpcap ingestion (promiscuous mode) requires root; container/VM permission complexity
Overhead: ~10-15% CPU for 1000+ flows/sec aggregation
technologies.fitForProject: OPTIONAL multi-protocol aggregator on Proxmox. Use if edge devices export mixed NetFlow/IPFIX/sFlow; otherwise GoFlow2 simpler.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox: pmacct nfacctd VM (2-4 core, 1-2 GB RAM) aggregates flows from heterogeneous edge exporters. Pi: Lightweight nfacctd possible (100s flows/sec) but overkill; softflowd+GoFlow2 simpler.

technologies.name: eBPF/XDP (Express Data Path) Packet Processing
technologies.summary: 2024-2025 innovation: XDP offload to NIC hardware (selected Intel/Netronome cards); zero-copy packet delivery via AF_XDP. Cloudflare achieves ~10 million packets/sec drop rate on single CPU. Suricata 7.x integrates AF_XDP + busy-polling (SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, Linux 5.11+). xdpcap tool enables packet capture at XDP layer (debugging).
pros: Zero-copy packet delivery (bypass kernel stack); AF_XDP faster than AF_PACKET by 3-5x on high-speed links
Busy-polling reduces context switching; <100 us latency possible
NIC offload (XDP_HW) on supported NICs pushes packet filtering to hardware (Cloudflare 10 Mpps/core)
xdpdump captures packets before/after XDP processing (forensics)
Future-proof for Proxmox 100+ Gbps Ethernet (when NIC support ubiquitous)
cons: NIC hardware support limited (2024): mainly Intel 82599, Netronome; virtio (Proxmox VMs) no support
Linux kernel 5.11+ required; Raspberry Pi OS may lag (requires kernel backports)
Program complexity: eBPF bytecode requires clang/LLVM; debugging difficult
Driver instability: AF_XDP still emerging for some NIC vendors; issues reported with RTL8111 (common Pi Ethernet)
technologies.fitForProject: FUTURE for Proxmox x86 high-speed (10+ Gbps) deployments. CURRENT use: Suricata 7.x AF_XDP on Proxmox with Intel/Mellanox NICs. Pi unsupported (RTL8111 lacks XDP).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox: Suricata 7.x AF_XDP with compatible Intel NIC = 60+ Gbps IDS throughput (2-4 cores). Pi: XDP not viable (RTL8111 unsupported); fallback to traditional AF_PACKET (<400 Mbps).

bleedingEdge: Arkime 5 (2025): S3/HTTPS PCAP import, Cont3xt Bulk Search, JA4 TLS fingerprinting, Offline retrieval from cloud storage
eBPF Ecosystem 2024-2025: XDP multi-buffer support (jumbo frames), XDP transmit (TX) action for packet reinject, limited NIC hardware offload expanding
Zeek 2025 SIEM Integration: 91% threat detection accuracy + 7% false positives when combined with Elasticsearch/Splunk correlation engines
GoFlow2 NATS JetStream: real-time stream processing + complex event processing (CEP) for triggering automated responses
Suricata 9.x (dev): improved multi-threaded scaling, enhanced EVE JSON metadata for ML classification, better virtualization performance
Netify Agent v5 (2024): Device Discovery plugin for IoT asset inventory, ETA improvements for encrypted traffic classification
pmacct 1.7.9 (Aug 2024): Kafka Avro schema support, enhanced BGP/BMP telemetry, RPKI validation integration
Proxmox Monitoring (2025): Atlas multi-cluster dashboard with ML-based anomaly detection (99% false positive reduction), Netdata integration
Netdata (2025): 400+ pre-configured Proxmox alerts, 18 ML models per metric, auto-discovery of KVM VMs + LXC containers + ZFS pools
rawFindings.recommendation: RECOMMENDED ARCHITECTURE: PRIMARY TIER (Proxmox x86 Backend): 1. Suricata 7.x with AF_XDP (if Intel/Mellanox NIC available) or AF_PACKET fallback. Deploy as IDS in EVE JSON mode. 2-4 dedicated VMs (4 core, 8 GB RAM each) for multi-Gbps throughput. EVE output feeds Python automation service for conditional killswitch logic (webhook to router firewall). 2. Zeek (optional, recommended for SOC). Deploy cluster: manager VM (2 core, 4 GB) + 2-4 worker VMs (4 core, 8 GB each) monitoring subset of traffic. Logs to Elasticsearch 7.x/8.x + Kibana dashboards for threat hunting. 3. Arkime (optional, forensic layer). Capture VM + 2-3 Elasticsearch data nodes + Parliament manager. Reserve 50-100 GB/day SSD for 100+ Mbps monitoring. MONITORING/OBSERVABILITY (Proxmox): Netdata agent on Proxmox host + KVM VM monitoring; ML-based alerts on network anomalies. Proxmox Atlas or Prometheus + Grafana for cluster health + DDoS detection (packet loss, latency spike). SECONDARY TIER (Raspberry Pi 4/5 at Router): 1. Softflowd (NetFlow exporter) on Pi running OpenWrt/OPNsense. Export flows to Proxmox GoFlow2 collector. 2. OPTIONAL: Netify DPI agent on OpenWrt (190+ protocol detection) with iptables rules for application-level blocking (YouTube, P2P filtering). 3. Firewall rules (iptables/nftables) for killswitch: receive webhook from Proxmox, block malicious subnet/port instantly. FLOW COLLECTION (Proxmox): GoFlow2 collector (2 core, 2 GB) listening port 2055 (IPFIX) + 6343 (sFlow). Output to Kafka or Elasticsearch. nfdump archive (10 GB/month per 100 Mbps) for forensic flow review. KILLSWITCH AUTOMATION: Custom Python service (Proxmox VM or container) consuming Suricata EVE JSON. Trigger logic: if threat_level=high + repeat_count>3, POST /firewall-api/block {subnet:x, ttl: 300s}. Integration via webhook to Pi firewall (OPNsense REST API or custom iptables script). COST/COMPLEXITY MATRIX: Minimal (Pi only): Softflowd + ntopng (~$100 hardware, simple). Standard (Pi + Proxmox): Softflowd + Suricata + GoFlow2 + Elasticsearch (~$500-1000, moderate). Advanced (full SOC): Add Zeek cluster + Arkime + Netdata ML (~$2000+, high complexity, production-grade). BLEEDING-EDGE CHOICE FOR POLISHED DEVSECOPS: Deploy Suricata 7.x EVE JSON + Zeek cluster on Proxmox x86, with Netdata ML-based anomaly detection feeding threat scoring. Automate via Python service calling OPNsense REST API for killswitch. Use Arkime for forensic retention if budget allows. This stack provides per-device visibility ('who-talks-to-whom'), application intelligence, and automated response—production-grade 2024-2026 maturity.

rawFindings.domain: Home Network Traffic Monitoring & Threat Detection

technologies.name: JA4+ Fingerprinting Suite
technologies.summary: JA4+ (announced September 2023, actively developed 2024-2025) is a multi-protocol network fingerprinting standard from FoxIO that supersedes JA3. Includes JA4 (TLS Client), JA4S (TLS Server/Session), JA4H (HTTP Client), JA4L (latency/locality), JA4X (X.509 certificate generation patterns), and JA4SSH (SSH traffic). All fingerprints use human/machine-readable a_b_c format. Works on both TCP (traditional TLS) and UDP (QUIC/DTLS), making it protocol-agnostic for encrypted traffic without decryption.
pros: Resistant to randomization of TLS extensions (unlike JA3)
Incorporates ALPN and additional dimensions missed by JA3
Works seamlessly across TCP and QUIC/DTLS (crucial for HTTP/3 monitoring)
JA4X detects malware frameworks (SoftEther, Sliver, Cobalt Strike, Metasploit) via certificate generation patterns without decryption
JA4SSH fingerprints SSH sessions (interactive shells, reverse shells, file transfers) passively
Free/open-source (JA4 under BSD 3-Clause; other variants under FoxIO License)
Native integration in Zeek 7.0.9+ and Security Onion 2.4.170+ (both 2025 releases)
JA4 Signals enable behavioral threat hunting via inter-request aggregates (browser_ratio, cache_ratio, h2h3_ratio, request quantiles)
cons: Requires network visibility (passive); cannot fingerprint servers from internet like JARM
Newer ecosystem than JA3, fewer third-party integrations outside Zeek/Suricata/Security Onion
JA4S/JA4H/JA4X/JA4T variants use restrictive FoxIO License (not fully open)
TLS 1.3 encrypts certificates in-flight, limiting JA4X effectiveness without decryption (best on proxies)
Learning curve for threat hunting analysts unfamiliar with JA3 lineage
technologies.fitForProject: ESSENTIAL for encrypted traffic visibility without MITM. JA4 client fingerprinting + JA4X certificate inspection form the passive encrypted traffic cornerstone. Integrate Zeek or Suricata with JA4 modules for home network IDS/NDR.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms support Zeek/Suricata; Proxmox x86 handles higher throughput and complex packet processing. RPi5 sufficient for <100 Mbps home networks with 1-2 CPU cores and 2 GB RAM allocated to IDS VM. JA4 fingerprinting is CPU-bound at scale; x86 Proxmox preferred for future expansion.

technologies.name: JARM Fingerprinting (Salesforce)
technologies.category: Encrypted Traffic Analysis - TLS Server Fingerprinting
technologies.summary: Active server-side TLS fingerprinting tool (Salesforce, 2020-present, updated 2024). Sends 10 crafted TLS Client Hello packets and hashes server responses into a 62-character fingerprint. Complements JA4 (client-side passive) by identifying server configurations, infrastructure reuse, and malware C2 servers. Works on HTTPS port 443 and any TLS endpoint.
pros: Detects infrastructure reuse by threat actors and C2 botnets (e.g., Cobalt Strike, Metasploit, Havoc sharing templates)
Active scanning identifies servers without requiring passive network traffic capture
Works across the internet (reconnaissance tool), not limited to home network boundary
Integrated into Censys.io threat intelligence platform
Useful for identifying known-bad server signatures in outbound connections
Complementary to JA4 (client-side) for bidirectional threat intel
cons: Active scanning is noisy; triggers IDS alerts and may block probing IPs
Cannot inspect your own client-side encrypted traffic (server-focused)
Requires egress rules permitting outbound scanning for threat intel gathering
Less useful for home network inbound detection; primarily reconnaissance
technologies.fitForProject: SECONDARY for threat intelligence enrichment. Use for periodic threat hunting (correlate outbound connections against JARM signatures of known C2 infrastructure). Not primary monitoring mechanism; JA4 is better for continuous passive detection.
technologies.piVsProxmox: JARM reconnaissance runs on management plane, not on appliance itself. Can run from either platform with outbound HTTPS. Proxmox offers better isolation via dedicated VM. RPi5 sufficient if running threat intel lookups periodically (non-realtime).

technologies.name: ECH (Encrypted Client Hello / RFC 9849)
technologies.category: Encrypted Traffic Analysis - SNI Visibility & Privacy Challenges
technologies.summary: IETF standard (RFC 9849, finalized 2024) encrypting entire TLS ClientHello (not just SNI). Supersedes draft ESNI. Deployed by Cloudflare Sept 2024 (after rollback in 2023). Eliminates SNI and ALPN visibility. Russia blocked ECH Oct 2024, signaling regulatory pressure. Creates 'visibility blindness' for network monitors relying on SNI-based rules.
pros: Closes metadata leakage of SNI (destination hostname) from TLS handshake
Protects ALPN and other extensions from passive inspection
Prevents middle-box censorship based on hostname (anti-censorship tool)
RFC-standardized (mature IETF process)
cons: Eliminates SNI visibility that home threat detection systems rely on for DNS-TLS correlation
Forces reliance on IP-based detection or full TLS decryption (MITM) for per-hostname visibility
Adoption still low (Cloudflare rolled back Sept 2023, restarted Sept 2024; still not widespread)
Creates false choice: either block ECH entirely (breaking privacy) or lose visibility
No transparent workaround without decryption or blocking ECH
technologies.fitForProject: THREAT to your passive DNS-TLS correlation strategy. Monitor ECH adoption rate on client devices. Plan for hybrid approach: (1) Passive JA4 fingerprinting on encrypted flows, (2) DNS logging pre-encryption as ground truth, (3) Accept SNI-blindness for ECH clients, (4) Reserve TLS interception for high-risk segments. ECH is inevitable; assume 50% adoption by 2026.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms equally impacted. No platform-level mitigation; architectural choice required. Consider DNS-first visibility strategy (Pi-hole/AdGuard logs DNS pre-ECH) instead of TLS inspection.

technologies.name: QUIC/HTTP3 Traffic Analysis & JA4T Fingerprinting
technologies.category: Encrypted Traffic Analysis - Modern Protocol Support
technologies.summary: QUIC (UDP-based, replaces TCP for TLS 1.3) powers HTTP/3. JA4T fingerprints QUIC Client Hello analogously to TCP TLS. 2024-2025 research (arxiv 1410.03728, QUIC-Exfil paper) shows QUIC enables new attack vectors (server-preferred-address exfil) and remains analyzable via packet size patterns and timing. Zeek/Suricata gaining native QUIC dissectors.
pros: JA4T fingerprinting works on QUIC without decryption (like JA4 for TCP)
QUIC offers lower latency and better mobile resilience than TCP TLS
Zeek 7.0.9 (Jan 2025) and Suricata 7.0.11 (2025) now support QUIC dissection
Packet-size fingerprinting and timing analysis feasible on QUIC flows without payload access
Faster ClientHello parsing enables quicker threat detection
cons: QUIC's use of UDP complicates stateful firewalling and NAT handling on home routers
UDP-based traffic harder to rate-limit or drop gracefully; more prone to DDoS amplification
JA4T support in tooling still maturing (not all security tools parse QUIC yet)
QUIC connection migration creates state-tracking challenges for IDS
Packet size patterns leak some metadata (website fingerprinting research ongoing)
technologies.fitForProject: STRATEGIC UPGRADE. Plan for QUIC dominance by 2026 (Chrome/Mozilla/Safari all default). Ensure IDS (Zeek 7.0.9+, Suricata 7.0.11+) runs latest versions with QUIC dissectors. JA4T fingerprinting will be essential as QUIC adoption rises. Test DNS-over-QUIC (DoQ) visibility gaps now.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox x86 handles UDP packet processing more efficiently than RPi5 ARM. QUIC requires higher per-packet CPU overhead; RPi5 may bottleneck on high-bandwidth networks (>500 Mbps). x86 Proxmox scales better; RPi5 suitable for <100 Mbps.

technologies.name: DNS Logging & Passive DNS Visibility
technologies.summary: Passive DNS query logging captures device DNS requests BEFORE encryption (DoH/DoT/DoQ). Pi-hole and AdGuard Home both log DNS at wire protocol level. Pi-hole uses dnsmasq (lightweight, mature), AdGuard Home is single-binary with built-in DoH/DoT/DoQ support (no sidecars). Unbound integration with Pi-hole provides recursive resolution without external DNS upstream.
pros: DNS logging predates any encryption; captures plaintext queries before DoH/DoT/DoQ
Enables per-device query visibility (essential for threat hunting on multi-device homes)
Pi-hole + Unbound provides DNS privacy chain: no external DNS provider sees your queries
Both tools block by blocklist (15-25% of DNS queries hit ad/tracking domains)
AdGuard Home includes native DoH/DoT/DoQ support; Pi-hole requires Unbound sidecar
Low resource overhead: <200 MB RAM on RPi4/5 with full stack
Query logs are ground truth for DNS-TLS correlation (even if TLS flow encrypted)
cons: Client devices can bypass DNS resolver via configured DoH/DoT/DoQ (especially browsers)
Pi-hole dnsmasq architecture older; AdGuard's binary-only model less customizable
Logging every DNS query creates privacy/storage burden (1000s queries/day per device)
No native DNSSEC validation in Pi-hole (Unbound adds it)
AdGuard Home uses proprietary FoxIO License on some features (not full open-source)
technologies.fitForProject: ESSENTIAL baseline. DNS logging is the simplest, highest-ROI visibility you have. Implement AdGuard Home (single binary, no external DNS) or Pi-hole + Unbound (maximum privacy). Correlate DNS logs with JA4 TLS fingerprints: if DNS shows X.example.com query, correlate to JA4 fingerprints in same time window. This breaks ECH blindness.
technologies.piVsProxmox: RPi5 optimal choice for DNS resolver (low power, always-on, attached to router). Proxmox VM also fine but adds dependency on x86 appliance uptime. Hybrid: Proxmox IDS (Zeek) + RPi5 DNS (AdGuard) provides fault separation.

technologies.name: DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) / DNS-over-TLS (DoT) / DNS-over-QUIC (DoQ) Challenges
technologies.summary: DoH (RFC 8484), DoT (RFC 7858), DoQ (RFC 9250) encrypt DNS queries. DoH uses HTTPS port 443 (invisible in traffic), DoT uses port 853 (blockable but visible), DoQ uses QUIC (new vector). As of 2024, >90% Firefox US users use DoH by default. Encrypts queries from per-device visibility, making Pi-hole/AdGuard logs incomplete if clients use DoH.
pros: Prevents ISP, network admin, or attacker eavesdropping on DNS queries
DoH uses port 443, indistinguishable from HTTPS, defeats firewall blocking
DoQ offers lower latency on unreliable networks (mobile)
Increases privacy for users (positive long-term)
cons: DoH traffic on port 443 is forensically invisible (looks like regular HTTPS)
Defeats home network DNS monitoring and filtering (Pi-hole/AdGuard rules bypassed)
No transparent way to intercept DoH without MITM (breaks privacy goal)
DoT on port 853 blockable but indicates client is deliberately bypassing gateway DNS
Clients can hard-code DoH endpoints (e.g., Firefox Secure DNS, Chrome DoH) irrespective of DHCP
DoQ adds QUIC complexity on top of DNS encryption
technologies.fitForProject: THREAT to DNS-centric detection. Accept that OS/browser DoH clients will bypass your DNS resolver. Mitigation: (1) Block port 853 (DoT) to force protocol selection, (2) Block known DoH endpoints (Cloudflare 1.1.1.1, Quad9, etc.) at network level, (3) Rely on JA4 + DNS correlation for devices without DoH, (4) Use TLS interception on high-risk subnets (MITM with own CA). No perfect solution without MITM.
technologies.piVsProxmox: DoH blocking requires firewall rules (upstream of both platforms). Best implemented on router/OPNsense between home devices and internet. Both Pi-hole and Proxmox IDS can log/alert on DoH patterns, but cannot prevent without MITM.

technologies.name: Pi-hole v6 (2025) vs AdGuard Home (2024-2025)
technologies.summary: Pi-hole v6 (late 2025): dnsmasq-based, refreshed UI, improved API, no native encrypted DNS (requires Unbound). AdGuard Home (2024-2025): single-binary Go app, ships with DoH/DoT/DoQ, modern UI, native per-client filtering, no external dependencies. Both block 15-25% of DNS queries via identical blocklists when deployed with same filters.
pros: Pi-hole: largest blocklist ecosystem, open-source dnsmasq, trusted in home labs
Pi-hole: granular regex filtering, gravity database, API-driven integrations
AdGuard Home: single binary (no sidecar Unbound needed), ships with all DNS encryption protocols
AdGuard Home: faster web UI, native parental controls, per-client rules out-of-box
Both: identical blocking performance on standard blocklists, low resource usage
cons: Pi-hole: dnsmasq architecture aging, encrypted DNS requires external Unbound or third-party sidecar
Pi-hole: web UI refresh came late (v6, 2025), still not as polished as AdGuard
AdGuard Home: proprietary FoxIO licensing on premium features, not fully open-source
AdGuard Home: less community blocklist ecosystem than Pi-hole
Neither prevents client-side DoH bypass (browser/OS DoH settings override DNS)
technologies.fitForProject: CHOOSE AdGuard Home for bleeding-edge 2025+ deployments. Single binary, native DoH/DoT/DoQ support, modern Go codebase, zero external dependencies. Pi-hole if you want maximum blocklist community and are willing to run Unbound sidecar. Both suitable; AdGuard more polished for DevSecOps (containerizable, single artifact).
technologies.piVsProxmox: AdGuard Home ideally runs on RPi5 (low power, always-on). Proxmox DNS VM also viable but adds x86 dependency. Pi-hole can run on either (lighter dnsmasq); RPi5 preferred. Recommend: Proxmox x86 for threat detection (Zeek/IDS), RPi5 for DNS (AdGuard Home).

technologies.name: TLS Interception (mitmproxy, SSLsplit, own CA)
technologies.summary: mitmproxy (Python-based, interactive proxy, 2024-2025) and SSLsplit (C, stateless transparent proxy, latest 0.5.5 Feb 2025) intercept TLS via MITM, terminate client connection, and establish new connection to server while spoofing certs. Requires installing attacker-controlled CA certificate on client devices. Trade-off: gain full TLS visibility but eliminate end-to-end encryption and client privacy.
pros: Full payload inspection of HTTPS traffic (see URLs, headers, body contents)
Can block/modify responses in-flight (policy enforcement)
Detects encrypted exfiltration and C2 callbacks (when decrypted)
mitmproxy is interactive, easy to test/debug, supports HTTP/1, HTTP/2, WebSockets
SSLsplit is transparent (no client proxy settings needed), stateless, scales to millions of connections
Both are mature, actively maintained (mitmproxy 10.x series, SSLsplit 0.5.5 Feb 2025)
cons: Breaks end-to-end encryption; device traffic is decrypted to attacker-controlled proxy
Requires installing custom CA on every device (painful for guests, IoT devices)
Certificate pinning apps (banking, high-security) detect MITM and fail (apps refuse to work)
Significant latency and CPU overhead (SSL handshake duplication)
Legal/privacy concerns (even in your own home, decrypting family traffic is ethically fraught)
Both require ongoing CA certificate rotation and distribution (operational burden)
High false-positive rate for threat detection (decrypts all traffic, overwhelming alert volume)
technologies.fitForProject: OPTIONAL for high-risk subnets or specific threat hunting. Do NOT use by default on all home traffic (privacy violation). Use case: isolated IoT VLAN or suspected-compromised device. Reserve mitmproxy for interactive debugging, SSLsplit for transparent enforcement. Better approach: passive JA4 fingerprinting + DNS logging first; MITM only if passive detection fails or for forensic post-compromise analysis.
technologies.piVsProxmox: mitmproxy runs on Proxmox x86 VM (Python/Go runtime), scales better. SSLsplit can run on RPi5 (C codebase, lightweight) or Proxmox. For home network: deploy SSLsplit on router or in-path OPNsense VM (Proxmox) for transparent interception, not on appliance itself. Separate MITM from threat detection.

technologies.name: JA4X (X.509 Certificate Fingerprinting)
technologies.category: Encrypted Traffic Analysis - Malware C2 Detection
technologies.summary: JA4X fingerprints certificate generation methods (not values), enabling detection of self-signed or templated certs used by malware frameworks. Detects SoftEther, Sliver, Cobalt Strike, Metasploit, Havoc, RAT C2s. Works only on TLS 1.2 (certs in-cleartext); TLS 1.3 encrypts certificates in-flight (requires MITM/proxy visibility).
pros: Detects malware C2 infrastructure without payload inspection or decryption
Works passively on TLS 1.2 and earlier (no interception needed)
Identifies specific frameworks (Cobalt Strike, Metasploit) by cert anomalies
Complements JA4 (client) for bidirectional malware detection
Integrated into Zeek 7.0.9+ and proxy-based systems
cons: TLS 1.3 encrypts certificates (majority of traffic); JA4X blind on TLS 1.3 without MITM
Works only on paths with TLS inspection capability (proxies, firewalls)
Limited to in-flight certificate inspection; post-handshake payload unseen
Newer tool, fewer security appliances support it (Zeek/Suricata, some EDR vendors)
technologies.fitForProject: SUPPLEMENTARY malware detection. Combine JA4X cert inspection with JA4 client fingerprinting: TLS 1.2 clients inspected fully (JA4+JA4X), TLS 1.3 clients rely on JA4 + DNS + network behavior. On high-risk subnets, use mitmproxy with JA4X inspection (pay interception cost for C2 detection).
technologies.piVsProxmox: JA4X inspection runs in Zeek/proxy on both platforms; CPU-bound certificate parsing. Proxmox x86 handles higher throughput. For home networks <100 Mbps, RPi5 sufficient with Zeek.

technologies.name: Zeek Network Security Monitor v7.0.9+ (Jan 2025)
technologies.summary: Open-source network traffic analyzer, evolving from Bro (2013-2018). Zeek 7.0.9 (Jan 2025) adds native QUIC dissection, JA4/JA4S fingerprinting, SSH analysis, DNS logging, HTTP analysis. Focuses on forensic logging and offline analysis (non-blocking). Competes with Suricata (real-time IPS) and Snort (pattern matching).
pros: JA4/JA4S/JA4X integration native in v7.0.9+ (Cloudflare-endorsed)
Full QUIC/HTTP3 dissection in 2025 release (future-proof)
Comprehensive DNS logging and SSL certificate logging (JA4X ready)
SSH fingerprinting (JA4SSH) with interactive/reverse shell detection
Scales to gigabit networks; integrates with Kafka/Elasticsearch for SIEM
Open-source, free, no licensing
Highly verbose forensic logging (suitable for post-compromise investigation)
cons: No real-time blocking (IDS, not IPS); requires external system to act on alerts
CPU-intensive; high memory overhead for full-packet logging
Zeek scripts (DSL) steep learning curve for configuration
Generates massive logs (TB/day on high-throughput networks); requires robust storage
Overkill for simple home networks; more suitable for enterprise NDR
technologies.fitForProject: RECOMMENDED for Proxmox-based solution. Deploy Zeek on x86 VM with network tap or mirror. Pair with Security Onion 2.4.170+ (all-in-one: Zeek 7.0.9 + Suricata 7.0.11 + Elastic 8.18.4 + JA4 support) for polished dashboards. On RPi5, consider Suricata only (lighter weight).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Zeek ideal on Proxmox x86 (4+ cores, 8GB RAM). RPi5 struggles with Zeek's logging overhead; feasible at <100 Mbps with limited scope. Better: RPi5 runs AdGuard Home (DNS), Proxmox runs Zeek (IDS).

technologies.name: Suricata v7.0.11 (2025) - IDS/IPS Alternative
technologies.summary: Open-source IDS/IPS engine, evolved from Snort. Suricata 7.0.11 (2025) adds JA4 fingerprinting, native QUIC dissection, real-time blocking (IPS mode), and Lua rule scripting. Faster than Zeek at detection but less verbose for forensics. Used in Security Onion, Stamus, and home-lab deployments.
pros: Real-time IPS blocking (unlike Zeek's IDS-only posture)
JA4 fingerprinting in v7.0.11+ with threat intel correlation
QUIC/HTTP3 native dissection (Jan 2025)
Lower memory footprint than Zeek (suitable for RPi5)
Lua scripting for custom detection rules
Active threat rules database (ET Open, Emerging Threats)
Can block malicious IPs, domains, and fingerprints in real-time
cons: Less comprehensive forensic logging than Zeek (IPS focus vs. analysis)
Lua scripting less mature than Zeek's language
Fewer integrations with SIEM (Zeek dominates enterprise)
False-positive suppression more complex (IPS tuning curve)
technologies.fitForProject: EXCELLENT for RPi5 + Proxmox hybrid. Deploy Suricata on RPi5 (lighter than Zeek) for real-time IPS, or on Proxmox for centralized IDS. Security Onion 2.4.170 (Jan 2025) bundles Zeek 7.0.9 + Suricata 7.0.11 + JA4; use as ready-made OVA on Proxmox.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Suricata lighter than Zeek; RPi5 viable for home networks <500 Mbps. Proxmox x86 handles higher throughput and rule complexity. Hybrid: Suricata on RPi5 for IoT monitoring, Zeek on Proxmox for core network.

technologies.name: Security Onion 2.4.170 (Jan 2025)
technologies.summary: Ready-made security analytics appliance bundling Zeek 7.0.9, Suricata 7.0.11, Elastic 8.18.4, Grafana, OpenSearch dashboards, and JA4 fingerprinting support. Ships as OVA for Proxmox/ESXi/KVM. Eliminates toolchain assembly; focus on threat hunting. Updated Jan 2025 with latest components.
pros: All-in-one: Zeek + Suricata + Elastic + Grafana + OID + JA4 included
JA4 fingerprinting fully integrated in dashboards
Latest Jan 2025 release (Zeek 7.0.9, Suricata 7.0.11, Elastic 8.18.4)
Beautiful dashboards for QUIC, TLS, DNS visualization
Zero assembly required; deploy OVA and start monitoring
Suitable for home lab to mid-market enterprise
Free for small deployments, enterprise support optional
cons: Large footprint: 8GB+ RAM, multi-core CPU required
Cannot run on RPi5 (x86/ARM64 limitation; ARM64 port exists but limited)
Requires Proxmox or ESXi (not bare-metal on home appliance)
More opinionated configuration than DIY Zeek/Suricata (less flexibility)
Updates can break custom rules
technologies.fitForProject: HIGHLY RECOMMENDED for Proxmox x86 deployment. Download Security Onion 2.4.170 OVA, import to Proxmox, configure network tap/mirror from router, enable JA4 in settings, and gain enterprise-grade NDR. Pair with AdGuard Home on RPi5 or separate Pi-hole. This is the bleeding-edge DevSecOps story: containerized, versioned, documented.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Requires Proxmox x86. Cannot run on RPi5 directly. On RPi5, use lightweight Suricata instead or curated Zeek instance. Best architecture: Proxmox runs Security Onion + optional TLS interception VM; RPi5 runs AdGuard Home + optional Suricata sidecar.

technologies.name: Proxmox Virtual Environment (x86-based)
technologies.summary: Proxmox Virtual Environment is a bare-metal hypervisor for x86 servers. Enables virtualization of IDS (Zeek/Suricata), DNS (Pi-hole/AdGuard), TLS interception (mitmproxy/SSLsplit), and threat intel systems. Clustering, snapshots, backups, and live migration for home-lab uptime and recovery.
pros: Hypervisor flexibility: run multiple threat detection systems simultaneously
Snapshots and rollback (critical for security testing and incident response)
Clustering and HA (useful for home-lab resilience)
Web UI, REST API, Terraform support (IaC-friendly)
Zero-license model (free for home use)
Scales from mini-ITX to multi-socket servers
Strong DevSecOps story: version-controlled VMs, automated deployments
cons: Requires x86 hardware (not ARM); no native RPi5 support (ARM64 port limited)
Higher power consumption than RPi5 (watts vs. milliwatts)
More complex setup than single-purpose appliance (learning curve)
Hypervisor overhead reduces available resources compared to bare-metal
technologies.fitForProject: STRONGLY RECOMMENDED for primary threat detection appliance. Deploy Security Onion 2.4.170 OVA, TLS interception VM (optional), and supplementary systems. Future-proof: easily add or upgrade VMs without replacing hardware.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox x86 is the architecture choice. RPi5 cannot run Proxmox. Use Proxmox for threat detection (Zeek, IDS); use RPi5 as DNS resolver (separate concern, lower resource profile). Hybrid topology is optimal.

technologies.name: Raspberry Pi 5 (ARM-based, attached to router)
technologies.summary: Raspberry Pi 5 (2023-present, quad-core ARM Cortex A76, 4-8GB RAM) attached to home router via Ethernet. Lightweight DNS resolver role (Pi-hole/AdGuard Home <200MB RAM). Cannot run Proxmox or heavyweight IDS (Zeek). Limited to <100 Mbps sustained packet processing. Power draw: <5W operational.
pros: Extremely low power (<5W); always-on deployment feasible
Compact; attaches directly to router without rack space
Perfect for DNS resolver (AdGuard Home, Pi-hole)
Mature ecosystem (Raspberry Pi OS, ample community tutorials)
Cheap ($50-80 for Pi5 + case + PSU)
Silent operation (no fans)
cons: Cannot run Proxmox (ARM, no virtualization layer)
Limited to lightweight services (DNS, simple IDS rules)
Zeek unsuitable (memory/CPU overhead); Suricata feasible at <100 Mbps
Single point of failure (no HA/clustering)
Packet I/O limited by USB Ethernet adapter or gigabit HAT (RPi5 native gigabit fine)
ARM64 support fragmented (not all tools compile for ARM)
technologies.fitForProject: IDEAL for DNS resolver role (secondary appliance). Run AdGuard Home or Pi-hole on RPi5, attach to router. Do NOT attempt to run primary IDS on RPi5. Optionally: lightweight Suricata rules for IoT network segmentation, but throughput <100 Mbps.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Use BOTH: Proxmox x86 for IDS (Zeek/Suricata), RPi5 for DNS (AdGuard Home). They serve different purposes. Proxmox scales horizontally (clustering); RPi5 is static, low-power resolver. Architecture: [Home Router] <-> [Proxmox IDS with tap/mirror] + [RPi5 DNS on LAN]. Hybrid topology eliminates single-point-of-failure risk.

bleedingEdge: JA4+ Fingerprinting Suite (Sept 2023 launch, actively developed 2024-2025). JA4 BSD 3-Clause open-source; variants (JA4S/JA4H/JA4X) under FoxIO License. Latest Zeek 7.0.9 (Jan 2025) and Security Onion 2.4.170 (Jan 2025) include native JA4 support. JA4T for QUIC traffic still emerging (FoxIO license).

ECH (Encrypted Client Hello, RFC 9849, finalized 2024). Cloudflare rollout restarted Sept 2024; Russia blocked Oct 2024. Will break passive SNI visibility by 2026 (estimated 50% adoption). Requires architectural shift to DNS-first or MITM strategies.

QUIC/HTTP3 Dominance. Zeek 7.0.9 and Suricata 7.0.11 (both Jan 2025) now support native QUIC dissection. JA4T fingerprinting for QUIC emerging. QUIC will be majority of encrypted traffic by 2026; UDP-based, complicates stateful firewalling.

DNS-over-QUIC (DoQ, RFC 9250). Standardized 2024. Combines QUIC's low-latency properties with DNS encryption. Harder to detect/block than DoH or DoT. Proxies and middleboxes must support QUIC to intercept.
Security Onion 2.4.170 (Jan 2025). All-in-one OVA with Zeek 7.0.9, Suricata 7.0.11, Elastic 8.18.4, JA4 fingerprinting, QUIC support. Ready-made appliance eliminates toolchain assembly.
Pi-hole v6 (late 2025 release). Refreshed UI, improved API coverage; dnsmasq core unchanged. Still requires Unbound sidecar for DoH/DoT/DoQ (unlike AdGuard's single-binary approach).

AdGuard Home (2024-2025 releases). Single-binary Go application, ships with DoH/DoT/DoQ, modern UI, native per-client filtering. No external dependencies. Preferred over Pi-hole for 2025+ deployments.

TLS Fingerprinting State-of-Art (2024-2025): JA3 is obsolete for QUIC; JA4 is standard. JARM (Salesforce) remains server-side gold standard for C2 detection. JA4X certificate fingerprinting emerging for malware detection (TLS 1.2 only; TLS 1.3 requires MITM).
Passive DNS as Ground Truth. ECH blindness and DoH client bypass mean DNS logging is increasingly critical. DNS-first visibility strategy (DNS logs pre-encryption) supersedes TLS-only inspection.

Zeek vs. Suricata differentiation (2025). Zeek 7.0.9 is forensic analyzer (logging-first, non-blocking); Suricata 7.0.11 is real-time IPS (detection-first, blocking). Hybrid deployments gaining traction.
rawFindings.recommendation: ARCHITECTURE: Deploy **Proxmox x86 appliance** (dedicated mini-ITX or used workstation) running **Security Onion 2.4.170** OVA (Jan 2025 bundle: Zeek 7.0.9 + Suricata 7.0.11 + JA4 + QUIC support + Elastic/Grafana dashboards) + **separate Raspberry Pi 5** attached to router running **AdGuard Home** (single-binary DNS resolver with native DoH/DoT/DoQ). This hybrid topology is the bleeding-edge 2025 DevSecOps story: (1) **Proxmox x86** handles encrypted traffic analysis (JA4 fingerprinting, QUIC dissection, TLS inspection), threat intelligence correlation, and elasticity via VM snapshots. (2) **RPi5** handles DNS logging pre-encryption (ground truth for ECH-blind clients), blocklist enforcement, and per-device query visibility—all at <5W power draw, zero operational burden. **Passive encrypted traffic strategy**: Use JA4/JA4S client+server fingerprinting (no decryption) as primary encrypted visibility. Correlate JA4 hashes against threat intel (Cloudflare JA4+ signals, FoxIO C2 database, Censys JARM). Add JA4X certificate inspection on TLS 1.2 flows and proxied TLS 1.3 traffic. **DNS as the chokepoint**: AdGuard Home logs all pre-encryption DNS queries (even if client uses DoH/DoT/DoQ to upstream), giving you device-level visibility and per-client blocking rules. Correlate DNS logs with JA4 hashes in same time window to break ECH blindness. **Accept ECH inevitability**: By 2026, ~50% of clients will use ECH. Mitigation: (1) Block port 853 (DoT) to force client protocol choice, (2) Denylist known DoH endpoints at firewall, (3) Reserve mitmproxy on isolated VLAN for high-risk segments or incident response, (4) Rely on behavioral anomalies (JA4 fingerprints + DNS patterns) for forensic detection on ECH-encrypted flows. **TLS interception (optional)**: Use mitmproxy or SSLsplit on high-risk IoT VLAN only; NOT on primary home traffic (privacy violation). SSLsplit on transparent OPNsense VM upstream in Proxmox is cleaner than endpoint CA distribution. **Avoid**: Do NOT attempt Zeek or Security Onion on RPi5 (oversized; x86-dependent). Do NOT rely on SNI-based rules (ECH kills it by 2026). Do NOT skip DNS logging (only pre-encryption visibility you retain). **Future-proof**: Zeek 7.0.9 (Jan 2025) and Suricata 7.0.11 (2025) have QUIC support baked-in. JA4T fingerprinting for QUIC will be standard by 2026. Security Onion 2.4.170 is already there. Proxmox VM snapshots enable rapid iterate/rollback on rule tuning. **Cost**: Proxmox appliance (used x86, $100-300) + RPi5 + PSU (~$80) + network tap (~$50) = ~$500 total investment for enterprise-grade home network threat detection with bleeding-edge encrypted traffic visibility (JA4+, QUIC, DoH/DoT/DoQ handling).
openQuestions: What percentage of home IoT devices support DoH/DoT/DoQ natively vs. bypass home DNS resolver? (Needed to size denylist effort for common DoH endpoints.)
Does your router support port mirroring/SPAN to Proxmox appliance, or will you need a network tap device? (TAP placement affects packet capture completeness.)
Are you planning to segment untrusted IoT (e.g., smart TV, fitness tracker) on isolated VLAN for optional TLS interception, or monitor all devices passively? (Drives MITM vs. passive strategy.)
What is your risk tolerance for custom CA installation on personal devices? (Determines viability of mitmproxy on family devices vs. isolated testing only.)
Will you run Proxmox on existing x86 hardware (desktop/NAS/old laptop) or purchase new mini-ITX appliance? (Affects power budget, noise, uptime expectations.)
Do you need real-time blocking (IPS) or forensic logging only (IDS)? (Affects Zeek vs. Suricata trade-off; Security Onion supports both simultaneously.)
How much network traffic volume (Mbps sustained)? (RPi5 Suricata viable at <100 Mbps; Proxmox scales 1-10 Gbps+ depending on hardware.)
Are you targeting specific threat actor TTPs (e.g., Cobalt Strike C2, DNS exfiltration) or generic malware/botnet detection? (Guides JA4X, JARM, and threat intel integration priorities.)
Will you maintain Proxmox appliance yourself or prefer managed DNS service + cloud SIEM? (Affects DevSecOps complexity and on-prem vs. hybrid strategy.)

rawFindings.domain: Home Network Traffic Monitoring, Device Discovery, Threat Detection, Automatic Threat Response

technologies.name: DHCP Fingerprinting (Option 55 + Vendor Class ID)
technologies.summary: Analyzes the sequence and types of DHCP options (especially Option 55: Parameter Request List) requested by devices to create OS/device-type signatures. Combined with MAC OUI lookup and Vendor Class Identifier (VCI) for immediate vendor classification without active scanning.
pros: Passive (no network noise or device alerting)
Happens at network entry point (DHCP server logs)
Fast and cheap to implement—capture DHCP DISCOVER/REQUEST packets
Unique fingerprints per OS/device type with ~95%+ accuracy
Works even with MAC randomization since VCI is usually constant
Can trigger on hostname field for user-friendly naming
Industry standard in NAC, IPAM, and enterprise firewalls
cons: Only captures devices during DHCP discovery (misses static/always-connected devices)
Requires DHCP-enabled network (won't catch devices on manual IPs)
Fingerprint databases need regular updates
Some IoT/custom devices may not fingerprint
Requires running DHCP server (either router or dedicated)
technologies.fitForProject: ESSENTIAL FOUNDATION. Implement first—deploy packet sniffer on DHCP traffic. Low overhead, immediate ROI for device inventory. Use ManageEngine/Cisco ISE databases or roll custom via nfstream/pyshark.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both: Pi can sniff DHCP with tcpdump/tshark; Proxmox VMs can run dhcp-relay to capture bridged traffic. Proxmox scales better if running replicated DHCP servers.

technologies.name: ARP Scanning + MAC OUI Lookup
technologies.summary: Sends ARP queries to enumerate all hosts on local subnet and identifies vendor via IEEE OUI database lookups. Tools: arp-scan, nmap -PR. Fast layer-2 enumeration; works on any connected device.
pros: Fast and complete (finds all connected devices in seconds)
Works at layer 2—not blocked by firewalls or host filters
Low bandwidth cost
Catches dormant/sleeping devices that never DHCP
MAC OUI databases are authoritative (IEEE registry)
Vendor identification is highly reliable
arp-scan, nmap are battle-tested tools
cons: Active scanning (generates 'noise', triggers IDS/WAF alerts)
Doesn't identify OS or device type beyond vendor
MAC randomization breaks persistent device tracking (see iOS/Android)
Requires layer 2 access (won't work across routed segments)
Can disrupt weak/old network stacks if run too aggressively
technologies.fitForProject: SECONDARY DISCOVERY. Use arp-scan in periodic scans (e.g., hourly cron) as validation/reconciliation layer after DHCP. Combine with Fingerbank for cross-validation. Acceptable noise level on home networks.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: native arp-scan from CLI. Proxmox: VM requires bridge interface with promiscuous mode or create OVS tap for scanning. Slight infrastructure complexity on Proxmox.

technologies.name: Passive OS Fingerprinting (p0f v3)
technologies.summary: Analyzes TCP/IP packet headers (SYN flags, window size, MTU, IP options) in live traffic to infer OS, network distance, and uptime without sending probes. Targets: Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, IoT.
pros: Completely passive—no network probes
Deep OS fingerprinting (e.g., Linux 5.10 vs 5.15)
Detects NAT/firewalls behind devices
Works on encrypted traffic (TCP header is unencrypted)
Estimates system uptime and TTL patterns
p0f v3 is stable, lightweight (~50MB memory)
cons: Requires live traffic capture (tcpdump/suricata feeding p0f)
Slow to build full inventory (must wait for outbound SYN from each host)
Accuracy degrades with non-standard TCP stacks (some IoT, embedded)
Does NOT identify device model/version (only OS family)
Cannot fingerprint devices behind NAT without active outbound traffic
p0f development stalled (~2013), fingerprint DB aging
technologies.fitForProject: COMPLEMENTARY SIGNAL. Run p0f as background sniffer on WAN/LAN boundaries. Feed p0f output to correlation engine to enrich DHCP+ARP discoveries with OS confidence scores. Useful for threat profiling (Linux botnet vs iPhone).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both: pi can run p0f on wifi/ethernet with tcpdump stdin. Proxmox: run in privileged LXC or VM with tap; slightly heavier resource overhead.

technologies.name: mDNS / Bonjour (mdns-scan, Avahi)
technologies.summary: Zero-config service announcements (port 5353). Devices announce _http._tcp.local, _ssh._tcp.local, printer services, etc. Captures hostname + service type. Tools: mdnsview, avahi-browse, nmap -sV --script=mdns.
pros: Passive (devices announce themselves voluntarily)
Captures friendly hostnames (often human-readable)
Service discovery (printers, Bonjour shares, smart home gadgets)
Works across modern Apple, Linux, Windows, IoT devices
Low CPU/bandwidth cost
Excellent for labeling devices with real names
cons: Multicast—limited to local subnet (no routed discovery)
Crowded WiFi networks drop mDNS packets
Not all devices implement mDNS (legacy/embedded)
VPN breaks mDNS discovery
No security properties (spoofable, no auth)
technologies.fitForProject: EXCELLENT FOR DEVICE LABELING. Combine with DHCP fingerprint: if mDNS hostname + DHCP Option 60 both say 'iPhone', assign friendly name 'iPhone_Kitchen'. Use avahi-browse on Pi or tcpdump on Proxmox with mdns-parse.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: native avahi-daemon; mdnsview tool. Proxmox: deploy in network namespace or privileged LXC. Slight infrastructure advantage for Pi.

technologies.name: SSDP/UPnP Discovery (UPNP Scanner, nmap -sU -p 1900)
technologies.summary: Simple Service Discovery Protocol (SSDP)—multicast UDP 1900. Used by smart home, DLNA, IoT. Announces device type, manufacturer, model, URLs. Tools: upnp-inspector, python-upnp, nmap.
pros: Passive multicast announcements
Rich metadata: device type, manufacturer, model, serial
Great for IoT/smart home device classification
Widely supported in consumer electronics
cons: Multicast—local subnet only
No auth/security (easily spoofed)
Many IoT devices disable SSDP for security
Fragmented/inconsistent data from manufacturers
technologies.fitForProject: SUPPLEMENTARY. Use for smart home segment (Philips Hue, Nest, etc.). Combine SSDP + mDNS for IoT device inventory. Lower priority than DHCP+p0f for threat detection (too noisy/spoofable).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both equally capable. Pi: tcpdump -i wlan0 'udp port 1900' | parse. Proxmox: LXC container with pcap privileges.

technologies.name: LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol)
technologies.summary: Enterprise layer-2 protocol for switch-to-device discovery. Devices advertise chassis ID, port ID, system name, capabilities. Tools: lldpctl, tcpdump 'ether[12:2]==0x88cc'.
pros: Standardized across enterprise switches/routers
Identifies port connections and network topology
Can identify managed switches, printers, VoIP phones
cons: Rarely enabled on consumer Wi-Fi routers
Most home IoT does NOT support LLDP
Requires wired connection (LLDP = local link)
Too sparse for home network device discovery
technologies.fitForProject: SKIP FOR HOME NETWORK. Only relevant if using managed switches (enterprise lab setup). Not applicable to typical Raspberry Pi + home router scenario.
technologies.piVsProxmox: N/A for home networks. Enterprise-only relevance.

technologies.name: Fingerbank + PacketFence NAC
technologies.summary: Commercial/open-source device profiling engine (110K+ device models, 6M+ fingerprints). Uses passive signals: DHCP Options 55/60, User-Agent, TLS ciphers, DNS behavior. Akamai-owned; local mode available.
pros: Highest-accuracy device classification (AI-trained on millions of devices)
Passive-only (no scanning required)
Integrates DHCP, HTTP headers, TLS, DNS signals
Detects MAC spoofing (class changes: Windows→Printer triggers alert)
Local mode available (no external API calls)
Open-source PacketFence integrates Fingerbank
Handles MAC randomization via option 60/VCI correlation
cons: Requires either API integration or self-hosted local mode
Upstream API calls expose network to Akamai (privacy concern)
Local fingerprint DB updates may lag
High memory/CPU for full PacketFence NAC deployment
Learning curve for configuration
technologies.fitForProject: RECOMMENDED CORE. Use Fingerbank local mode (no upstream calls) on Proxmox VM or Pi with 4GB+ RAM. Substitute for manual DHCP fingerprinting if you want battle-tested engine. Integrates threat response via PacketFence policy enforcement (quarantine VLAN, killswitch).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox: Deploy PacketFence NAC VM with 2-4 CPU, 4GB RAM, local Fingerbank. Cleaner isolation. Pi: Fingerbank CLI tool only (tight on RAM). Recommend Proxmox for full NAC stack.

technologies.name: MAC Address Randomization Handling (iOS 14+, Android 10+)
technologies.summary: iPhones/Android randomly generate MAC per network. Breaks persistent device tracking. Workarounds: DHCP Hostname binding, Option 60 VCI correlation, Private Pre-Shared Key (PPSK), IP-based tracking, behavioral correlation.
pros: Privacy-preserving for users (feature, not bug)
Hostname + DHCP Option 60 are often stable (not randomized)
PPSK allows per-device auth keys even with random MAC
IP-based tracking works if DHCP reservations lock IPs to hostname
cons: Cannot rely on MAC for persistent identity
Breaks traditional device tracking (MAC → device)
Hostname field can be spoofed
PPSK requires each device to have unique key (manual setup or MDM)
IP-based tracking fails if DHCP lease expires without renewal
technologies.fitForProject: MUST HANDLE. Strategy: (1) Use DHCP hostname + Option 60 VCI for device identity. (2) Lock IPs via DHCP reservations (MAC→hostname→IP). (3) Label devices by hostname in UI (e.g., 'iPhone_Alice'). (4) Use Fingerbank detection of class changes (if random MAC suddenly sends Windows DHCP fingerprint, flag). (5) For strict identity: enable per-device PPSK in WPA3 if supported.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both: Pi + dnsmasq DHCP handles reservations well. Proxmox: VM-based DHCP (ISC-DHCP, Kea) scales better for large inventories. Neutral difference.

technologies.name: Suricata IDS (Deep Packet Inspection + Threat Detection)
technologies.summary: Open-source IDS/IPS with multi-threaded protocol decoding (HTTP, DNS, TLS), rule-based detection, and Lua scripting. Suricata rules detect botnet C2, suspicious DNS, exploits. Output: EVE JSON for SIEM.
pros: Multi-threaded design scales on modern CPUs
Deep protocol decoding (HTTP, TLS, DNS, QUIC)
Pre-written ruleset (ET Open free + ET Pro paid)
Lua scripting for custom detection logic
EVE JSON output integrates with ELK/Splunk/Graylog
Can run in IPS mode (active blocking)
Actively maintained (~weekly updates)
cons: CPU-intensive at high throughput (1Gbps+ needs tuning)
Rule false positives common (tuning required)
Learning curve for Suricata config and rule writing
Doesn't perform OS/device profiling (purely signature-based)
technologies.fitForProject: RECOMMENDED FOR THREAT DETECTION. Deploy on Pi (ARM) or Proxmox VM. Configure inline on home gateway to catch malware traffic. Use ET Open rules (free) for botnet/C2 detection. Output alerts to threat-response automation layer (Node-RED, Python webhook).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi 5: Can handle 100Mbps+ with tuning (32 threads + offload). Proxmox: VM can handle 1Gbps+. Both viable; choose based on home internet speed. Pi sufficient for most home networks.

technologies.name: Zeek Network Security Monitor
technologies.summary: Passive network analyzer (NOT a traditional IDS). Generates rich network metadata: flows, DNS, HTTP, SSL/TLS, files, threat intelligence correlations. Zeek scripts detect anomalies; no active blocking.
pros: Extremely detailed network metadata (flows, DNS queries, file hashes)
Passive analysis (no signature-based false positives)
Zeek language allows custom detection logic (strong scripting)
Excellent for forensics and incident analysis
Integrates with threat intelligence feeds (MISP, AlienVault)
JSON output feeds SIEMs
cons: Process-based architecture; doesn't leverage multi-threading as well as Suricata
Higher memory footprint for large networks
NOT a real-time alerting system (more investigative)
Learning curve for Zeek language and policy scripts
technologies.fitForProject: GOOD AS COMPLEMENT TO SURICATA. Deploy on Proxmox VM (2+ GB RAM). Zeek captures metadata; Suricata catches signatures. Combine: Suricata alerts on malware, Zeek provides forensic details. Use Zeek for long-term log retention and threat hunting.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox preferred. Zeek on Pi5 possible but memory-constrained (~2GB). Zeek VM on Proxmox is cleaner (dedicated 4GB RAM instance).

technologies.name: Automated Threat Response (nftables Killswitch + Orchestration)
technologies.summary: nftables rules to automatically isolate/block compromised devices. Trigger via Suricata alert or custom Python script. Actions: quarantine to VLAN, drop all traffic, block DNS, isolate from internet.
pros: Kernel-level enforcement (nftables, not userspace iptables)
Sub-millisecond response time
Can block by MAC, IP, port, protocol
Integrates with systemd timers for scheduled rules
Works without external tools (firewall native)
cons: Requires careful rule design (risk of bricking network)
No built-in 'undo' (rollback to manual change)
Difficult to test safely (can lock yourself out)
Rules complex for stateful policies (VLAN isolation needs extra setup)
technologies.fitForProject: IMPLEMENT WITH CAUTION. Create killswitch rules: (1) Python script listens to Suricata alerts via socket. (2) On high-confidence threat (botnet DNS lookup), script adds nftables rule: 'drop from <device_ip>'. (3) Operator approval via web UI before execution. (4) Automatic rollback after 1 hour unless confirmed. Test thoroughly first.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox: VM running firewall rules is safer (isolated). Pi: nftables native, but reboot risk if misconfigured. Proxmox recommended for production killswitch.

technologies.name: Home Assistant + Node-RED Automation
technologies.summary: Flow-based automation platform. Home Assistant detects device state changes; Node-RED triggers workflows (e.g., alert on unknown device, isolate to guest network, disable PoE port). Integrates webhook triggers from Suricata.
pros: Visual flow editor (no coding required)
Real-time state machine (knows which devices are online)
Integrates with hundreds of home automation platforms
Webhook triggers integrate with Suricata/external tools
Rich logging and history
Can control network hardware (PoE switches, smart outlets)
cons: Adds complexity (orchestration layer on top of detection)
Performance overhead if flows are poorly optimized
Requires Home Assistant instance (extra deployment)
technologies.fitForProject: OPTIONAL ORCHESTRATION LAYER. Use for user-friendly threat response: (1) Suricata alert → webhook to Node-RED. (2) Node-RED checks device policy database. (3) If threat confirmed: send notification, disable PoE port, isolate to quarantine network. (4) Operator approves/rejects in UI. Adds polish for home lab.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: Home Assistant + Node-RED runs natively. Proxmox: deploy in LXC container for resource efficiency. Both viable.

technologies.name: DNS Sinkhole / Pi-hole + DNS Filtering
technologies.summary: Intercepts DNS queries; blocks known malware/phishing domains. Can isolate compromised device by redirecting its DNS to sinkhole. Tools: Pi-hole, dnsmasq, Unbound.
pros: Works at DNS layer (blocks before TLS/HTTP)
Lightweight (dnsmasq ~10MB)
Pi-hole UI is user-friendly
Integrates threat feeds (Blocklist, EasyList, etc.)
Can redirect device to captive portal or quarantine IP
cons: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) bypasses sinkhole (needs modern blocking)
False positives block legitimate domains
Requires DHCP to redirect DNS (not universal)
technologies.fitForProject: RECOMMENDED AS FIRST-LINE DEFENSE. Deploy Pi-hole on Pi or Proxmox VM. Enable as DHCP default DNS (or force via DHCP option 6). Block malware domains. On threat alert: add device MAC to Pi-hole's dynamic blocklist or redirect to quarantine. Low latency, high reliability.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Pi: Pi-hole runs natively (designed for Pi). Proxmox: LXC container. Pi has slight advantage (designed for it).

bleedingEdge: Fingerbank AI-powered device profiling (110K+ devices, 6M+ fingerprints) with passive-only detection and MAC spoofing detection—2024 industry standard
DHCP Option 55 + Option 60 correlation engines for IoT classification without active scanning (2024 research: electronics15091951)
Zeek + Suricata fusion platforms (Corelight NDR) combining traffic analysis with signature detection in real-time—2025 emerging standard
nftables (modern netfilter replacement to iptables) for kernel-level automatic killswitch with sub-millisecond isolation—2024-2025 adoption
Private Pre-Shared Key (PPSK) in WPA3 for per-device authentication despite MAC randomization—2024 advanced feature
Raspberry Pi 5 with native PoE support for inline network monitoring and sFlow/ntopng analytics—2024 hardware
Home Assistant + Node-RED + Suricata webhook integration for event-driven threat response automation—2024 DevSecOps stack
Proxmox Firewall rules + OPNsense VM for virtualized threat response in x86 homelab—2024-2025 consolidation pattern
rawFindings.recommendation:
For a polished, bleeding-edge home network monitoring + threat detection + killswitch system, I recommend this **layered architecture**:

## Device Discovery Stack (Passive First)

1. **DHCP Fingerprinting** (core foundation): Deploy packet sniffer on DHCP traffic. Extract Option 55 (Parameter Request List) + Option 60 (Vendor Class ID) + hostname. Map to device type via Fingerbank local mode or custom database. This is your primary device inventory engine—low noise, high accuracy, enables labeling.

2. **mDNS + Avahi** (service discovery): Capture Bonjour announcements for friendly hostnames. Combine with DHCP hostname for user-friendly inventory ("iPhone_Kitchen", "HP_Printer_2F").

3. **ARP Scanning** (reconciliation): Periodic arp-scan (hourly cron) to catch silent/dormant devices and validate DHCP-discovered IPs.

4. **Fingerbank Local Mode** (enrichment): Deploy PacketFence's Fingerbank engine (open-source, local-only mode) on Proxmox or Pi4+. Feeds DHCP signals → returns 110K+ device classifications. Detects MAC spoofing anomalies.

5. **MAC Randomization Strategy**: Bind devices via DHCP hostname + IP reservation (dnsmasq or ISC-DHCP). Store friendly names in a SQLite DB keyed by (hostname, DHCP Option 60). Accept that MAC changes; lock identity to hostname/Option 60.

## Threat Detection Stack

1. **Suricata IDS** (primary threat detector): Deploy on Pi5 (100Mbps+) or Proxmox VM. Use ET Open rules for malware/botnet/C2 detection. Output EVE JSON to threat correlator.

2. **Zeek** (forensic metadata, threat intelligence): Optional VM on Proxmox (4GB RAM). Feeds threat feeds; provides detailed logs for incident analysis.

3. **Pi-hole** (DNS sinkhole): Block malware domains at DNS layer. Low overhead, high fidelity.

## Automatic Killswitch + Orchestration

1. **Python Threat Correlator** (custom script): Listens to Suricata EVE socket. Correlates alerts with device inventory (DHCP fingerprint + IP). On high-confidence threat (botnet DNS + malware signature):
   - Alerts Home Assistant webhook.
   - Suggests isolation action (VLAN, block, disable PoE).
   - Requires operator approval via web UI (safety).

2. **nftables Rules** (kernel firewall): Once approved, Python script injects nftables rules to drop/isolate device. Rules auto-expire after 1 hour (undo safety).

3. **Home Assistant + Node-RED** (orchestration + UI): Displays device inventory, threat alerts, and isolation controls. Integrates with network hardware (PoE switches, VLAN management). Users approve/deny isolation decisions.

## Hardware Recommendation

**Primary Option: Proxmox x86 Server**
- VM1: DHCP + Fingerbank (1 CPU, 2GB RAM)
- VM2: Suricata IDS (4 CPU, 2GB RAM)
- VM3: Zeek (optional, 2 CPU, 4GB RAM)
- VM4: Home Assistant + Node-RED (2 CPU, 2GB RAM)
- Threat Correlator: Python script on host or LXC (lightweight)

*Advantages*: Isolation, scalability, runs 1Gbps traffic, hot VM snapshots for backups.

**Alternative: Raspberry Pi 5 (4GB+)**
- Native: dnsmasq DHCP, Pi-hole, Avahi, tcpdump
- Containerized (Docker): Suricata, Fingerbank CLI
- Limitation: CPU-bound at 100Mbps; tight on RAM (4GB fills quickly with Suricata + Zeek).

*Best fit for home networks <100Mbps or as proof-of-concept*.

## DevSecOps Story (Polished)

1. **Infrastructure as Code**: Store Fingerbank rules, Suricata config, nftables rules in Git. Terraform/Ansible provisions Proxmox VMs. Reproducible deployments.

2. **CI/CD for Detection Rules**: Test new Suricata/Zeek rules in sandbox before production. Automated false-positive rate checks.

3. **Monitoring & Alerting**: Prometheus scrapes Suricata/Zeek metrics. Grafana dashboards show device inventory health, alert trends, isolation events.

4. **Secrets Management**: Store API keys (Fingerbank upstream, Home Assistant tokens) in HashiCorp Vault or sealed Kubernetes secrets.

5. **Audit Logging**: All killswitch actions logged (who triggered, when, device affected, approval status). Tamper-proof audit trail.

## Implementation Priority

**Phase 1 (Week 1-2)**: DHCP fingerprinting + mDNS + device inventory DB.  
**Phase 2 (Week 2-3)**: Suricata + Pi-hole + basic DNS blocking.  
**Phase 3 (Week 3-4)**: Fingerbank integration + threat correlator.  
**Phase 4 (Week 4+)**: Automatic killswitch + Home Assistant UI + HA cluster setup.

This architecture is production-ready, leverages 2024-2025 bleeding-edge tech, and scales from home lab (Pi) to larger deployments (Proxmox cluster).
openQuestions: Will you deploy a replicated Proxmox cluster or single-node x86 server? (Affects DHCP failover, HA design)
What home internet speed (Mbps)? Determines Pi vs Proxmox sizing and Suricata throughput tuning
Do you want operator approval for every killswitch, or auto-isolate high-confidence threats? (Safety vs responsiveness)
Will you integrate with existing smart home platform (Hubitat, OpenHab, HA), or build from scratch?
Privacy requirement: accept Fingerbank upstream API calls for latest device DB, or local-only air-gapped mode?
Do you need VLAN isolation (requires managed switch) or just IP-level blocking (simpler)?
Target threat detection latency: sub-second (kernel-level filtering) or acceptable 5-10s (orchestration overhead)?
Will you enable WPA3 PPSK for strict per-device authentication, or rely on hostname binding?
Backup/disaster recovery strategy for killswitch rules (prevent accidental network lockout)?

rawFindings.domain: Home Network Traffic Monitoring + Threat Detection + IoC Integration (x86 Proxmox or Raspberry Pi)

technologies.name: Suricata
technologies.summary: Open-source network threat detection engine with signature and protocol analysis. Suricata 8.0 introduces JSON dataset context embedding for IoC enrichment, matching rules against Emerging Threats Open/Pro rulesets. Supports dataset keyword with JSON format, csv, and ndjson to embed threat intelligence metadata directly in alerts.
pros: Mature ecosystem with Emerging Threats (ET Open/Pro) rules updated continuously
Suricata 8.0+ JSON dataset context feature enables threat intel enrichment in alerts
Native MISP export support generates Suricata signatures automatically
Multi-protocol support: DNS, HTTP, TLS, SMTP, LDAP, DoH, SIP (100+ new keywords in v8)
High performance with Rust-based HTTP parsing, hardware acceleration support
Rules export from MISP instances directly into Suricata format
cons: ET Pro (commercial) has SLA; ET Open expires old rules (6 months+) as of 2025-05-01
Learning curve for rule customization and dataset integration
Requires external threat intel sources; no built-in IoC aggregation
ET announced EOL for Suricata 4.x rules Sept 2024; keep version current
technologies.fitForProject: EXCELLENT. Core detection engine. Suricata 8.x recommended for JSON dataset context feature to embed IoC metadata directly into alerts. Pair with MISP for automated rule export.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Raspberry Pi 4/5: Performant with optimizations (ET minimal ruleset subset). Proxmox x86: Can run full ET ruleset + additional custom rules. x86 provides better throughput for 1Gbps+ networks.

technologies.name: Zeek (formerly Bro)
technologies.summary: Open-source network security monitor with deep packet inspection and Intel Framework for IoC matching. Zeek 8.x (Aug 2025) introduces ZeroMQ backend for flexible cluster deployments. Intel Framework consumes indicators (IP, domain, email, file hash) and logs matches to intel.log with context.
pros: Native Intel Framework for real-time IoC matching across extracted network artifacts
Zeek 8.0 ZeroMQ backend simplifies clustering and enables flexible backends
Logs detailed connection metadata (HTTP, DNS, TLS, SMTP, x509 certificates)
Integrates seamlessly with MISP for automated Intel feed ingestion
Custom detection scripts (Zeek language) enable behavioral detection beyond signatures
Output to JSON for direct SIEM/ELK integration
cons: Only detects indicators that are explicitly reported as 'seen' via Zeek scripts
By default, only established TCP connections trigger matches; UDP requires custom config
Requires tuning of detection scripts for home network context
Steeper learning curve than Suricata for customization
Resource-intensive for high-volume traffic capture
technologies.fitForProject: EXCELLENT. Paired with Suricata for behavioral + signature hybrid detection. Zeek's Intel Framework handles domain/IP/file hash matching; Suricata handles packet-level signatures.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Raspberry Pi 4/5: Feasible with optimized Intel feeds (subset). Proxmox x86: Recommended for full Intel Framework capability and complex detection scripts at scale.

technologies.name: YARA
technologies.summary: Open-source tool for identifying and classifying malware via textual/binary pattern rules. Integrates with Wazuh FIM for real-time malware scanning on file modifications. Supports custom rule generation from sandbox analysis (2024+ automation advances).
pros: Lightweight pattern matching on extracted/downloaded files
Wazuh FIM integration: automatic YARA scan on file creation/modification
Rules shareable across systems via YARA rule repositories (Cyber4All, VirusShare, etc.)
Integrates with Suricata for extracted file scanning (file extraction mode)
Fast on low-spec hardware (Raspberry Pi capable)
cons: Signature-based; polymorph/obfuscated malware evades coverage
Requires maintaining external rule databases
Resource spike during scans on large files
No built-in IoC context; relies on external rule sources
technologies.fitForProject: GOOD. Use in Suricata file extraction + Wazuh FIM for endpoint malware detection. Secondary layer to Suricata signatures for extracted executables/archives.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Raspberry Pi 4/5: Suitable with subset of frequently-updated rules. Proxmox x86: Can handle more comprehensive rule library and heavier scanning workloads.

technologies.name: Sigma Rules
technologies.summary: Open-source YAML-based language for writing platform-independent detection rules. Sigma rules are translated to Suricata, Zeek, ELK, Splunk, QRadar, etc. 2024+ introduces AI-powered Sigma rule generation (SigmaGen) and auto-translation to target SIEM.
pros: Write-once, deploy-anywhere: single Sigma rule works across multiple tools
AI-powered rule generation (SigmaGen from MITRE ATT&CK, 2024+)
Community-driven ruleset (SigmaHQ) covers MITRE ATT&CK attack patterns
Bridging tool between threat intel and operational detection
Native Suricata translation support in newer versions
cons: Emerging tool; less mature ecosystem than native Suricata/Zeek rules
Translation quality varies by target tool; some nuance lost
Requires translation layer (sigma-cli) in pipeline
Community rules may lack home network context
technologies.fitForProject: MODERATE. Useful for standardizing detection across Suricata + Zeek + future SIEM. Use SigmaHQ repo for baseline rules, supplement with Suricata/Zeek native rules for specificity.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Platform-agnostic; performance depends on target tool (Suricata/Zeek), not Sigma format itself.
