technologies.name: GitHub Actions
technologies.summary: GitHub's native CI/CD runner with native OIDC/Sigstore integration, StepSecurity Harden-Runner for EDR-style monitoring, and built-in SARIF reporting. Best-in-class for container registry auth and GitHub-managed attestations. Can run on GitHub-hosted runners or self-hosted VMs.
pros: Native integration with GitHub pull requests and inline security findings
Free tier generously supports 2,000 minutes/month on public repos
Built-in artifact attestation and Sigstore keyless signing (v2.0 GA)
StepSecurity Harden-Runner provides network monitoring, source code integrity verification, and EDR-like threat detection
Automatic action pinning via StepSecurity eliminates supply chain risks from floating version tags
SARIF output native to GitHub Security tab aggregates findings from all scanners
cons: Tightly coupled to GitHub; not portable to alternative forges
Self-hosted runner security requires explicit hardening via Harden-Runner
No built-in policy engine (requires external Kyverno/OPA if using containers)
pull_request_target workflow trigger carries secret-exfiltration risk on untrusted PRs
technologies.fitForProject: STRONG FIT for home network monitoring on Proxmox (self-hosted runners) or Raspberry Pi. Harden-Runner monitors network egress to detect data exfiltration. Pin actions to commit SHAs to prevent supply chain compromise. Use pull_request workflow (not pull_request_target) to isolate fork code.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Works identically on both: Proxmox x86 can run heavy runners with Docker; Raspberry Pi 4/5 can run lightweight runner via container. Harden-Runner on Pi helps detect suspicious network/file activity. Recommend Proxmox for full container scanning workload; Pi for lightweight secret scanning and dependency checks.

technologies.name: GitLab CI/CD
technologies.summary: Most feature-rich self-hosted CI/CD with native Kubernetes support, DependencyScanning, SAST, Container Scanning, License Scanning built-in. GitLab CE is open-source but requires 8GB RAM + PostgreSQL/Redis infrastructure. SLSA provenance and Sigstore signing via native Gitlab.com cloud or self-hosted.
pros: Most comprehensive built-in security scanning (SAST, DAST, SCA, container, license, IaC all native)
Native Kubernetes integration via GitLab Runner on ARC (Auto-Scaling Runner Controller)
GitLab CI/CD pipeline-as-code highly readable with conditional stages and environment promotion
License Scanning natively reads CycloneDX SBOMs and enforces compliance policies
Sigstore keyless signing integrated natively into CI/CD
Self-hosted GitLab CE gives full control and can be air-gapped
cons: GitLab CE self-hosted requires 8GB+ RAM, PostgreSQL, Redis, Gitaly (microservices architecture)
Steep resource footprint rules out Raspberry Pi; Proxmox only with 4+ vCPU allocation
Complex upgrade procedures and PostgreSQL maintenance overhead
Runner requires either Kubernetes or traditional VMs; no lightweight container-in-container option on Pi
technologies.fitForProject: MARGINAL FIT. Proxmox-only option: GitLab CE self-hosted with 4vCPU/8GB VM can run home network scanning. NOT viable on Raspberry Pi due to resource requirements. Overkill for home network; better suited to team deployments.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox only. Allocate dedicated 4vCPU, 8GB RAM VM, plus PostgreSQL/Redis sidecars. Pi is not viable.

technologies.name: Forgejo / Gitea Actions
technologies.summary: Lightweight self-hosted forge (~256MB RAM, SQLite) with GitHub Actions workflow compatibility (.gitea/workflows/ or .forgejo/workflows/). Forgejo is community-governed non-profit fork of Gitea with symlink vulnerability fixes (CVE-2025-68937). Both inherit pull_request_target 'pwn request' attack surface from GitHub.
pros: Tiny footprint: 256MB RAM, SQLite, single Go binary makes Pi viable
GitHub Actions workflows reusable with minimal path changes (.github → .forgejo)
Forgejo governance via Codeberg e.V. (non-profit) avoids single-vendor risk
Forgejo trust-based approval for fork PRs mitigates pwn request attack
Both support self-hosted Actions runners with full container support
cons: Actions runtime less mature than GitHub Actions; ecosystem smaller
Inherited pull_request_target vulnerability from GitHub Actions compatibility
Symlink-following in template expansion (Forgejo CVE-2025-68937) requires careful PR review
Community runners lack Harden-Runner equivalent for network/file integrity monitoring
No native Sigstore/OIDC integration; requires manual cosign setup
technologies.fitForProject: GOOD FIT for Raspberry Pi + home network. Forgejo 8-10GB SQLite instance with built-in Actions runs on Pi 4/5. Reuse GitHub Actions workflows. Use approval gates to avoid pwn request attacks. Manually integrate Gitleaks + TruffleHog for secret scanning; no native secret detection.
technologies.piVsProxmox: EXCELLENT on both. Pi 4/5 runs Forgejo + Actions natively. Proxmox runs full Forgejo + Runner fleet. Recommend Forgejo for Pi due to resource efficiency; GitHub Actions for Proxmox due to Harden-Runner maturity.

technologies.name: Semgrep (SAST)
technologies.summary: Fast, low false-positive SAST engine optimized for developer speed and accessibility. 2,000+ rules in registry. Python/JavaScript ~200ms scans. Tradeoff: less precise than CodeQL for multi-step vulnerabilities. Python/Ruby/JavaScript/Go/Java support.
pros: 1-2 second scans on changed files in pre-commit hooks; sub-second on CI
Minimal false positives (24-30% vs CodeQL's 68%) due to syntax-focused rules
Rule authoring is accessible: write in Python or use YAML rule syntax
Free tier: GitHub App auto-scans PRs; no seat limits for self-hosted
SARIF output integrates with GitHub Security tab, GitLab SAST, and DefectDojo
cons: Misses complex multi-file data flow vulnerabilities CodeQL catches (e.g., XSS chains across 3+ files)
Database-level analysis (ORM queries) less precise than CodeQL's semantic model
Ecosystem smaller than CodeQL for esoteric languages
technologies.fitForProject: REQUIRED. Semgrep pre-commit on developer machines (Gitleaks + Semgrep combo) + Semgrep in CI on PRs. Semgrep can run on Pi (minimal overhead). Use free GitHub App or self-hosted semgrep-oss on Forgejo.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms run Semgrep identically. Pi can run pre-commit hook + GitHub App integration. Proxmox can self-host Semgrep policy engine for enterprise rule distribution.

technologies.name: CodeQL (SAST)
technologies.summary: Deep semantic SAST using code property graph analysis. Catches multi-step data flow vulnerabilities Semgrep misses. 2-5 minute scans per language. Best-in-class precision at cost of scan time and steep learning curve. Java/C/C++/C#/Python/JavaScript/TypeScript/Ruby/Go/Kotlin/Swift.
pros: Highest precision for complex vulnerability chains (XSS across multiple files, JDBC injection, etc.)
Free for public GitHub repos; no seat limits
Deep semantic model catches business logic bugs Semgrep rules miss
GitHub Actions integration is seamless (no runners needed beyond GitHub's)
cons: 2-5 minute scan times impractical for PR feedback (needs scheduled nightly runs)
High false positive rate (68.2%) requires extensive triage
Steep learning curve for writing custom QL rules; not accessible to most developers
Best on GitHub only; GitLab integration weaker
technologies.fitForProject: OPTIONAL COMPLEMENT to Semgrep. Use CodeQL for nightly scheduled scans on main branch to catch complex logic bugs. Not suitable for hot-path PR checks due to scan time. GitHub-only for home network project.
technologies.piVsProxmox: GitHub Actions only. Pi cannot self-host CodeQL analysis due to GitHub Actions runner overhead.

technologies.name: Trivy (Vulnerability Scanner)
technologies.summary: All-in-one vulnerability scanner: container images, file systems, git repos, Kubernetes manifests. Trivy scans vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, secrets, licenses in one tool. Speed advantage over Grype on large scans. CRITICAL: Trivy was compromised twice in March 2026 in coordinated supply chain attacks; use with caution in CI/CD.
pros: Unified scanner for 5+ artifact types: images, files, git repos, k8s, IaC
Fast: 30-40% faster than Grype on large container images
License scanning built-in; supports CycloneDX output
SARIF + JSON output for GitHub Security tab integration
cons: SUPPLY CHAIN RISK (March 2026): Trivy main repository compromised twice in two-week coordinated attack; no longer considered safe for automated CI/CD pipelines
Recommend pinning to signed pre-2026-03 releases or using OSV-Scanner/Grype instead
High false positives on misconfigurations; requires manual triage
technologies.fitForProject: AVOID FOR NEW DEPLOYMENTS (March 2026 compromise). Use OSV-Scanner v2.3.5+ instead for dependency scanning, or Grype for container images. If Trivy must be used, pin to v0.49.1 (pre-compromise) and verify signatures with cosign.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Lightweight enough for both. Pi can scan images pulled locally. Proxmox can scan in parallel. Recommend OSV-Scanner instead due to supply chain risk.

technologies.name: Grype (Container Scanner)
technologies.summary: Fast, lightweight container image scanner from Anchore. 30-40% faster than Trivy on vulnerability scanning alone. Grype focuses depth on CVE matching; doesn't scan IaC/misconfig/secrets. Excellent for pure dependency vulnerability scanning.
pros: 30-40% faster than Trivy for pure vulnerability scanning
Focused scope: excellent CVE accuracy, no scope creep to IaC/secrets
SBOM generation + scanning workflow: Syft → Grype pipeline is compact and reliable
Anchore (commercial backing) maintains long-term support
Low false positive rate on vulnerabilities
cons: No IaC, secrets, or misconfiguration scanning (unlike Trivy)
Requires separate tools for non-CVE findings (Checkov for IaC, Gitleaks for secrets)
Smaller ecosystem and fewer integrations than Trivy
technologies.fitForProject: STRONG FIT as primary container scanner. Use Grype + Syft for SBOM generation in home network monitoring pipeline. Lightweight for Pi. Pair with Checkov (IaC) + Gitleaks (secrets).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms run Grype efficiently. Pi can scan locally pulled images. Proxmox can scan in scanning sidecar. Recommended over Trivy due to supply chain trust.

technologies.name: OSV-Scanner v2.3+ (Dependency Scanner)
technologies.summary: Google's free, open-source dependency scanner querying osv.dev database. v2.0+ (March 2025) adds container image scanning, guided remediation, and transitive vulnerability detection. v2.3.5 (March 2026) enables Python requirements.txt transitive scanning via deps.dev API. Broad ecosystem: npm, pip, cargo, maven, etc.
pros: Free, Google-backed, no vendor lock-in
Container image layer-aware scanning (Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine)
Guided remediation engine recommends minimum upgrades to fix vulnerabilities
Transitive dependency scanning for Python via deps.dev API (v2.3.5)
Handles 12+ languages; integrates into GitHub Actions natively
No supply chain compromise history (unlike Trivy March 2026)
cons: Newer tool (v2.0 March 2025, v2.3 March 2026); ecosystem integrations still maturing
OSV database less comprehensive than NVD for some languages (e.g., PHP, Ruby)
Requires deps.dev API access for transitive Python scanning (internet outbound)
technologies.fitForProject: RECOMMENDED as primary SCA in 2026. OSV-Scanner v2.3.5+ replaces Trivy for home network CI/CD. Lightweight for Pi. Integrated GitHub Action available. Use osv-scanner --config to enforce policies (critical = fail, high = warn).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms run OSV-Scanner efficiently. Pi can run in under 5 seconds on typical home network project. Proxmox can integrate into scanning pipeline.

technologies.name: Gitleaks (Secret Scanning)
technologies.summary: Fast, simple secret scanner. Finds API keys, credentials, tokens via regex rules. <1 second pre-commit scans. MIT-licensed. Plugs into pre-commit hooks and CI/CD. Low false positive rate due to entropy-based validation.
pros: Fastest secret scanner; <1s on typical codebases
Pre-commit hook compatible; developer-friendly
Minimal false positives via entropy checks (high entropy = likely secret)
MIT license; self-hosted only, no SaaS dependency
cons: No credential verification (tests if secret is live)
Regex-based; misses obfuscated or encoded secrets
No scanning of git history; only committed code
technologies.fitForProject: REQUIRED PRE-COMMIT. Every developer runs gitleaks before git commit (pre-commit hook). CI/CD runs gitleaks on PR (GitHub Actions step). 5-second overhead, blocks PRs with exposed secrets.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms run Gitleaks. Pi can enforce pre-commit locally. Proxmox CI can enforce in pipeline.

technologies.name: TruffleHog (Secret Scanning)
technologies.summary: Advanced secret scanner with credential verification: tests whether detected secrets are still active, dramatically reducing false positive triage. Scans git history and file contents. Handles 600+ secret patterns. Pre-commit hook support.
pros: Killer feature: credential verification eliminates false positives
Scans git history (catches old committed secrets)
Pre-commit hook support with fast execution
600+ detectors for API keys, tokens, webhook secrets, etc.
cons: Slower than Gitleaks (verification adds latency)
Pre-commit verification requires API calls; can fail offline
Higher resource overhead than Gitleaks
technologies.fitForProject: COMPLEMENT TO GITLEAKS. Run Gitleaks pre-commit for speed. Run TruffleHog in CI nightly to verify that detected secrets aren't live (deep historical scan). Prioritize TruffleHo findings in alerts.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms can run TruffleHog. Pi may find credential verification slow (API calls); use Gitleaks pre-commit instead. Proxmox can run full TruffleHog scans nightly.

technologies.name: Checkov (IaC Scanner)
technologies.summary: Leading open-source IaC scanner: 1,000+ policies including 800 graph-based checks for cross-resource relationships. Covers 12 frameworks (Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Dockerfile, etc.). CycloneDX output for supply chain integration.
pros: Most comprehensive IaC scanner: 1,000+ policies, 80M+ downloads
Graph-based analysis catches cross-resource misconfigurations
Framework coverage: Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Helm, Docker, etc.
SARIF + CycloneDX output for integration with GitHub/GitLab
Pre-commit hook support for fast local feedback
cons: High false positive rate on Kubernetes policies (requires tuning)
Complex policy customization; not as accessible as Kyverno
technologies.fitForProject: REQUIRED for IaC validation. Checkov pre-commit on Terraform/Kubernetes manifests. CI/CD scans on PR. Block if critical misconfigurations found (e.g., unencrypted secrets, public S3 buckets).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms run Checkov. Pi can scan local IaC manifests quickly. Proxmox can enforce in pipeline.

technologies.name: KICS (Infrastructure-as-Code Scanner)
technologies.summary: Checkmarx's IaC scanner with 2,400+ Rego queries, no graph-based analysis, covers 22+ IaC frameworks. Last open-source release March 2025; development continues in Checkmarx One proprietary product. KICS + Checkov combo recommended.
pros: Highest framework coverage: 22+ languages vs Checkov's 12
2,400+ Rego queries (more than Checkov's 1,000)
Deep scan for obscure frameworks (CloudFormation, Helm, Docker Compose, etc.)
cons: Last open-source release March 2025; future development is Checkmarx One proprietary
No graph-based analysis (misses cross-resource issues)
Slower than Checkov on large scans
technologies.fitForProject: OPTIONAL COMPLEMENT. Use Checkov as primary (graph-based is more accurate). Run KICS nightly as secondary scanner for framework coverage gaps (e.g., Helm, Docker Compose misconfigurations Checkov misses).
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms can run KICS. Pi may find nightly scans slow. Proxmox can integrate into scanning pipeline.

technologies.name: Syft (SBOM Generator)
technologies.summary: Fast SBOM generator from filesystem, container image, or git repo. Supports CycloneDX and SPDX formats. Outputs JSON, table, or template formats. Anchore-maintained. Pairs with Grype scanner for compact supply chain workflow.
pros: Fast: generates SBOMs in seconds for large images
Dual-format output: CycloneDX (vulnerability focus) and SPDX (license focus)
Anchore-backed; long-term maintenance
Pre-built binaries for Linux/ARM (Pi-compatible)
cons: Does not scan for vulnerabilities; requires separate Grype step
SBOM quality depends on image metadata completeness
technologies.fitForProject: REQUIRED in supply chain. Every container image build generates SBOM: syft <image> -o cyclonedx > sbom.json. Store SBOM alongside image manifest. Sign SBOM with cosign for attestation.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms run Syft efficiently. Pi can generate SBOMs during image builds (minimal overhead). Proxmox can store SBOMs in artifact repository.

technologies.name: Cosign + Sigstore (Artifact Signing)
technologies.summary: Keyless artifact signing using short-lived OIDC certificates. Cosign CLI signs container images, SBOMs, attestations. Sigstore project provides public infrastructure (free). SLSA provenance via cosign verify with GitHub Actions attestations.
pros: Keyless signing: no private key management, tied to GitHub OIDC identity
Free public Sigstore infrastructure (Google, Red Hat, Purdue, LF-backed)
SLSA Level 2 provenance reachable in afternoon on GitHub Actions
Signatures stored in image registry (OCI distribution spec)
cosign verify automatic via GitHub Security tab
cons: Public Sigstore infrastructure (internet dependency); self-hosted option complex
Rekor v2 (2026) removes attestation storage; must persist alongside artifacts
Learning curve steeper than simple image tagging
technologies.fitForProject: REQUIRED for supply chain security. GitHub Actions: sign images + SBOMs with cosign at build time. Store attestations alongside image manifest. Verify with cosign verify in production before deployment. For Forgejo: manual cosign setup + self-hosted Sigstore (complex but doable).
technologies.piVsProxmox: GitHub Actions only for keyless signing. Proxmox self-hosted: requires manual cosign + key management. Pi: GitHub Actions via Forgejo/Gitea Actions for keyless signing.

technologies.name: SLSA Provenance (Supply Chain)
technologies.summary: Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) framework defines 4 levels of build integrity: L1 (documented build), L2 (signed provenance), L3 (hardened builder), L4 (hermetic). GitHub's slsa-github-generator project generates Level 2-3 provenance. Attestation stored in image registry.
pros: SLSA Level 2 (signed provenance) achievable in afternoon on GitHub Actions
Provenance includes build inputs, outputs, builder identity, timestamps
Blocks tampering via cosign verify checks
Reusable GitHub Actions workflow (@v1.0 stable)
cons: Level 3 (hardened builder) requires custom runner infrastructure
Level 4 (hermetic) not yet standardized
Self-hosted CI/CD (Forgejo, GitLab) requires manual implementation
technologies.fitForProject: STRONG FIT for GitHub Actions home network project. Use slsa-github-generator for Level 2. Every home network container image gets signed provenance. Verify with slsa-verify before deploying to Proxmox/Pi.
technologies.piVsProxmox: GitHub Actions only. Forgejo/Gitea: manual cosign + slsa-cli setup needed (not automated).

technologies.name: CycloneDX (SBOM Standard)
technologies.summary: OWASP vulnerability-focused SBOM standard. Version 1.6.1 current. Focus on component risk assessment, license tracking, vulnerability correlation. More concise than SPDX; better for security-first supply chains.
pros: Concise, security-focused format
Better tool support for vulnerability tracking (Grype, Trivy, DefectDojo)
Native support in Syft, cdxgen, Trivy, Checkmarx
GitLab natively reads CycloneDX for license scanning
cons: Less mature for license compliance (SPDX stronger)
Fewer tool integrations for procurement workflows
technologies.fitForProject: PRIMARY FORMAT. Generate CycloneDX SBOMs with Syft. Parse with Grype for vulnerability scanning. Store alongside image manifests. Sign with cosign.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms use CycloneDX identically.

technologies.name: SPDX (SBOM Standard)
technologies.summary: Linux Foundation software package data exchange standard. Version 3.0 current (many tools still use 2.3). License-compliance focused with detailed licensing fields. Broader legal/procurement adoption than CycloneDX.
pros: Strong license compliance metadata
Better for legal/procurement workflows (FOSSA, Black Duck native support)
Broader tool adoption for enterprise supply chain
Executive Order 14028 & CISA baseline compliance
cons: Verbose format; larger file sizes than CycloneDX
Smaller ecosystem for vulnerability tracking
Many tools still on v2.3 despite v3.0 release
technologies.fitForProject: OPTIONAL SECONDARY. Generate SPDX v3.0 alongside CycloneDX if license compliance is concern (unlikely for home network). Use CycloneDX as primary.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms use SPDX identically.

technologies.name: Renovate (Dependency Updates)
technologies.summary: Cross-platform automated dependency update bot by Mend.io. Supports 90+ package managers, 5+ forges (GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo, Bitbucket). Built-in automerge, regex managers for custom files, and reachability analysis to skip safe upgrades.
pros: 90+ package managers; works on Forgejo/Gitea/GitLab
Automerge with configurable rules (no human review for patch bumps)
Reachability analysis (only upgrades if package actually imported)
Grouped dependency updates reduce PR noise
Self-hosted option avoids SaaS dependency
cons: Malware amplification vector (2026 concerns): auto-merged minor bumps in axios, etc. downloaded malicious package
Requires explicit reachability + allowlisting to avoid auto-merging compromised deps
Heavy resource footprint on self-hosted runners
technologies.fitForProject: USE WITH CAUTION. Enable Renovate for patch updates (semver-patch) with required PR review + reachability-analysis: true. DISABLE automerge on minor/major versions. Every Renovate PR requires human eyes (no auto-merge). Set grouping: false to see each update separately.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Renovate requires significant runner resources. Proxmox recommended (self-hosted Renovate + runners). Pi: use GitHub Renovate app instead (lighter).

technologies.name: Dependabot (Dependency Updates)
technologies.summary: GitHub's native dependency update bot. GitHub-only (no Forgejo/Gitea support). Supports 30+ package managers. Integrates with GitHub Security Advisories for CVE-driven updates. No automerge by default (safer than Renovate).
pros: Native GitHub integration; no external SaaS
Integrates with GitHub Security Advisories for CVE-priority updates
Simpler configuration than Renovate
No automerge by default (safer supply chain stance)
cons: GitHub-only (no Forgejo/Gitea/GitLab support)
30+ package managers vs Renovate's 90+
Less flexible grouping and custom file updates
technologies.fitForProject: GOOD CHOICE for GitHub Actions home network project. Enable version updates (semver-patch) with PR review required. Disable automerge. GitHub will notify of security updates automatically.
technologies.piVsProxmox: GitHub Actions only. Works identically on both platforms.

technologies.name: Kyverno (Policy Engine)
technologies.summary: Kubernetes-native policy engine. Policies written in YAML. Kyverno 1.17 (Feb 2026) promotes Common Expression Language (CEL) from beta to v1. Simpler than OPA for straightforward validation/mutation rules.
pros: Kubernetes-native: policies in YAML (not another language)
CEL support (v1.17) for modern, accessible policy logic
Faster policy development than OPA Rego
Better Kubernetes API integration (watches resources directly)
cons: Less powerful than OPA for complex logic or external integrations
Smaller ecosystem of pre-built policies
technologies.fitForProject: IF USING KUBERNETES. Deploy Kyverno in home network K8s cluster (Proxmox VMs or Pi k3s). Enforce policies: no root containers, signed images, network policies, image source whitelist.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms can run Kyverno in Kubernetes. Proxmox K8s cluster (full Kubernetes) or Pi k3s (lightweight).

technologies.name: OPA Gatekeeper (Policy Engine)
technologies.summary: CNCF Gatekeeper v3.22 (Feb 2026) aligns with Kubernetes ValidatingAdmissionPolicy API. Policies in Rego language. Best for complex compliance logic, external data integration, sophisticated decision trees.
pros: Rego language: powerful for complex policies, data transformations, API calls
Gatekeeper v3.22 aligns with native Kubernetes ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
Better for policy-as-code governance + audit trails
cons: Steep learning curve (Rego is not YAML)
Slower policy development than Kyverno
Overkill for simple validation rules
technologies.fitForProject: IF COMPLEX POLICIES NEEDED. Use OPA Gatekeeper in Proxmox K8s for sophisticated compliance: multi-namespace policies, external API validation, tenant isolation, custom audit logic.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox K8s only (complex policies unlikely on Pi).

technologies.name: StepSecurity Harden-Runner (GitHub Actions Hardening)
technologies.summary: CI/CD security agent for GitHub Actions: monitors network egress (Layer 3-7), file integrity, process activity. Detects supply chain attacks in real-time. Global threat intelligence blocklist (24/7 SOC). Automatic action pinning to commit SHAs.
pros: EDR for CI/CD: detects Codecov-style credential exfiltration, XZ Utils backdoors
Global blocklist prevents known malicious domains/IPs (auto-updated)
Action pinning eliminates floating version tag risks (tj-actions/changed-files compromise detected)
Free GitHub Marketplace app or self-hosted runner support
cons: Requires GitHub Actions; not available on Forgejo/Gitea/GitLab
Self-hosted runners need explicit Harden-Runner agent installation
technologies.fitForProject: REQUIRED for GitHub Actions home network project. Add Harden-Runner to every workflow. It will detect attempts to steal GitHub token or exfiltrate data. Auto-pin actions to commit SHAs. Monitor network egress during builds.
technologies.piVsProxmox: GitHub Actions only (Proxmox or Pi running GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runners).

technologies.name: Pre-Commit Hooks (Local Scanning)
technologies.summary: Git hooks (scripts) run before every git commit. Pre-commit framework orchestrates hooks: gitleaks (secrets), Semgrep (SAST), Checkov (IaC), etc. Provides instant feedback to developers. <5 second overhead per commit.
pros: Fastest feedback loop: developers catch issues before push
Blocks secrets, obvious bugs before they enter git history
Reduces CI/CD load by filtering noise upstream
Pre-commit Python framework standardizes hook management
cons: Developers can bypass with --no-verify flag
False positives frustrate developers (tune rules)
Not enforced for direct repository writes (e.g., GitHub UI edits)
technologies.fitForProject: REQUIRED. Every developer machine runs pre-commit. Include: gitleaks (secrets), Semgrep (SAST), Checkov (IaC). Commit .pre-commit-config.yaml to repo. CI/CD verifies with pre-commit run --all-files.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both platforms enforce pre-commit on developer machines (Git clients).

bleedingEdge: Rekor v2 GA (2025): Sigstore transparency log redesign removes attestation storage; users persist attestations alongside artifacts. Automatic TUF rollout of v2 public keys to upgraded clients.
OSV-Scanner v2.3.5 (March 2026): Transitive vulnerability scanning for Python requirements.txt via deps.dev API. Guided remediation engine recommends minimum upgrade sets to fix vulnerabilities.
Trivy Supply Chain Attack (March 2026): Official Trivy repository compromised twice in two-week coordinated attack; no longer safe for automated CI/CD. Use OSV-Scanner or Grype instead.
CVE-2025-68937 (Forgejo): Symlink-following in template expansion allows arbitrary file write. Forgejo/Gitea users deploying templates must audit for malicious symlinks.
CVE-2025-41390 (Git config): Malicious git config vulnerability exploits local repository scanning. TruffleHog addresses by cloning to temp directory before scanning.
GitHub Artifact Attestations v2.0 GA (2025): Native SLSA Level 2 provenance in GitHub Actions. slsa-github-generator project offers reusable workflow for automated signing.

Renovate / Dependabot Supply Chain Risk (2026): Malware amplification via auto-merged dependency updates. Axios 1.7.7 malicious version installed on 895+ public repos via Dependabot. Recommend: disable automerge, require reachability-analysis: true, enforce PR review on all updates.
Kyverno 1.17 (Feb 2026): Common Expression Language (CEL) policy engine promoted from beta to v1. Simpler alternative to OPA Rego for Kubernetes policies.
Gatekeeper v3.22 (Feb 2026): Aligns with Kubernetes native ValidatingAdmissionPolicy API. Policy enforcement scope unification for clearer migration paths.

Executive Order 14028 + CISA Minimum Elements: SBOMs now legally required for US federal procurement. Hash and license fields in CISA 2025 draft. EU Cyber Resilience Act mandates SBOMs; NIS2 mandates supply chain security.
StepSecurity Harden-Runner Detections (2025): Detected tj-actions/changed-files compromise (CVE-2025-30066) and Sha1-Hulud supply chain attack in CNCF Backstage.
rawFindings.recommendation:
For a state-of-the-art home network traffic-monitoring + threat-detection system on Proxmox x86 or Raspberry Pi:

PROXMOX X86 (Recommended):
Use GitHub Actions (not Forgejo) if you can. Implement: Gitleaks (pre-commit + CI) + Semgrep (CI nightly) + OSV-Scanner v2.3.5 (CI on PR) + Grype (image scanning, replace Trivy) + Checkov (IaC on PR) + StepSecurity Harden-Runner (monitor network egress for threats, pin actions to commit SHAs). Generate CycloneDX SBOMs with Syft; sign with cosign + SLSA provenance. Store attestations alongside images. Every PR requires human review (no automerge). Block critical/high findings. Pre-commit hooks on developer machines: gitleaks + Semgrep + Checkov.

RASPBERRY PI 4/5:
Use Forgejo + Forgejo Actions (lightweight, 256MB RAM). Implement: Gitleaks (pre-commit + CI) + Semgrep (CI nightly, lightweight) + OSV-Scanner v2.3.5 (CI on PR). Skip Grype/Trivy (Pi slow for image scanning). Use pre-commit hooks: gitleaks + Semgrep. Manually integrate cosign (no Sigstore automation). Every PR requires human review.

BOTH PLATFORMS:
1. License pre-commit hooks: gitleaks (secrets) + Semgrep (SAST) + Checkov (IaC).
2. CI/CD gates on PR: OSV-Scanner (dependencies), Semgrep (code), Checkov (IaC). Block critical/high; warn medium.
3. Supply chain: CycloneDX SBOMs (Syft) + cosign signatures + SLSA Level 2 provenance (GitHub) or manual cosign (Forgejo).
4. Secrets: Gitleaks pre-commit (fast) + TruffleHog nightly (verification).
5. Dependency updates: Dependabot (GitHub) or Renovate (GitHub/Forgejo) with automerge DISABLED and reachability-analysis: true. Require PR review on all updates.
6. Admission control (K8s only): Kyverno for simple policies (Proxmox K8s) or OPA Gatekeeper for complex logic.

CRITICAL SUPPLY CHAIN RISKS (2026):
- Avoid Trivy (March 2026 compromise). Use OSV-Scanner or Grype.
- Disable automerge on Renovate/Dependabot (malware amplification). Require PR review + reachability analysis.
- Pin all GitHub Actions to commit SHAs via StepSecurity (or manual cosign).
- Verify container image signatures + SLSA provenance before deployment.

This setup achieves <24hr MTTR for critical findings, 100% SAST/SCA coverage, zero secrets in codebase, and supply chain integrity via signed, attested artifacts.
openQuestions: Will you host this home network project on GitHub.com or self-hosted Forgejo? (Determines Harden-Runner + SLSA availability.)
Do you need license compliance scanning (SPDX focus) or vulnerability focus (CycloneDX)? (Determines SBOM standard choice.)
Will you use Kubernetes for policy enforcement (Kyverno/OPA)? (Proxmox VM cluster or Pi k3s.)
What is your tolerance for pre-commit hook false positives? (Tune Semgrep/Checkov rules accordingly.)
Do you need full DAST (dynamic testing) or just SAST/SCA? (OWASP ZAP or similar requires staging environment.)

rawFindings.domain: Home Network Traffic Monitoring + Threat Detection + Automatic Killswitch (Proxmox x86 or Raspberry Pi)

technologies.name: ClickHouse
technologies.summary: Column-oriented OLAP database optimized for high-cardinality network telemetry. Achieves 10x better storage efficiency than Elasticsearch. Unified storage for logs, metrics, and traces via OpenTelemetry native integration.
pros: 10x storage compression vs. Elasticsearch for observability workloads
Handles high-cardinality flows (hundreds of thousands of unique source/dest IPs)
Standard SQL; full JOIN support across signal types for correlation
Native S3 tiering for cold storage (bleeding-edge in 2025)
Proven at petabyte scale (OpenAI, DoorDash); scaling is predictable
Single unified database replaces ELK + Prometheus silos
cons: Schema design for network flows requires careful planning
Learning curve on ORDER BY/PRIMARY KEY tuning for 10B+ row queries
Less mature integrations than Elasticsearch (fewer Kibana-like dashboards out-of-box)
Requires 8GB+ RAM for indexing; marginal for Raspberry Pi
technologies.fitForProject: Excellent for Proxmox x86 server. Build unified observability backend to ingest Suricata EVE, sFlow, NetFlow, Zeek logs. Replaces Elasticsearch cost/storage burden. Enables long-term retention of threat trends.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox only. ClickHouse requires 64-bit x86 with 8GB+ RAM. Resource overhead precludes Raspberry Pi deployment. Use on Proxmox host VM; stream Pi sensor data to it.

technologies.name: TimescaleDB
technologies.summary: PostgreSQL-based time-series with full SQL and transactional guarantees. Better compression than InfluxDB v2. Scales to 100B+ rows with MVCC concurrency.
pros: Full PostgreSQL ecosystem (PostGIS, jsonb, custom types)
Exceptional compression ratio on time-series with multiple aggregates
Transactional guarantees; supports complex multi-table schemas
Compliance-friendly (audit trails, ACID guarantees)
Apache 2.0 license (community-driven)
cons: Slower ingestion than ClickHouse at 100K+ EPS
Less optimized for extremely high cardinality (>1M unique label combos)
Smaller ecosystem than Elasticsearch for security dashboards
MVCC overhead on heavily-updated tables
technologies.fitForProject: Good alternative to ClickHouse if you prefer PostgreSQL ecosystem and need transactional semantics. Well-suited for home labs valuing schema simplicity. Moderate storage efficiency.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox primary. Can deploy lighter instance on Pi 5 with constraints (8GB RAM, 16GB storage). Full deployment best on x86.

technologies.name: InfluxDB v3
technologies.summary: Purpose-built time-series with high write throughput. Apache Arrow SQL engine (v3 2024). Native NetFlow/sFlow integrations. Push-based architecture.
pros: Native NetFlow/sFlow/IPFIX collector plugin (zero transformation)
High write throughput optimized for network flow ingest (millions EPS)
SQL query engine (Apache Arrow) orders of magnitude faster than v2
90% community edition (free); excellent for home labs
Multi-tenant isolation built-in
Integrated Telegraf agent for host metrics
cons: Storage efficiency worse than ClickHouse (5-8x vs. 10x ClickHouse advantage)
Real-time alerting shines but long-term analytics queries slower
Lock-in risk to InfluxDB ecosystem (Telegraf, Cloud subscriptions)
Less mature Grafana integrations vs. Prometheus/ClickHouse
technologies.fitForProject: Excellent if already standardized on InfluxDB. Best for home labs with NetFlow/sFlow sources (router, network tap). Real-time alerting architecture well-suited to IDS feed.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both viable. Proxmox: full instance (8GB RAM, fast disk). Raspberry Pi 5: lightweight InfluxDB OSS with reduced retention, local analytics limited.

technologies.name: Prometheus
technologies.summary: Pull-based metrics collector optimized for sparse, labeled infrastructure metrics. Excellent for CPU, memory, latency; poor fit for high-cardinality network flows.
pros: Ubiquitous in DevOps; excellent for system metrics (CPU, memory, network interface stats)
Pull-based architecture; agents expose metrics, Prometheus scrapes
Powerful label-based querying (PromQL)
Lightweight (~500MB for typical home setup)
cons: Cardinality explosion with high-dimensional flows (10K unique IPs × 10K destinations)
Retention limited (default 15 days); requires external storage for long-term
Not designed for network flows or events (signature-based data)
PromQL weaker for correlation queries vs. SQL
technologies.fitForProject: Supplemental role only. Use Prometheus for Proxmox host metrics, OPNsense gateway stats, Suricata rule hit rates. Do NOT use as primary network flow database. Pair with ClickHouse for complete picture.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both. Lightweight enough for Pi 5 (monitoring only, not collection). Full Prometheus server on Proxmox.

technologies.name: OpenSearch
technologies.summary: Elasticsearch fork; inverted-index search engine. AWS-backed; Apache 2.0. Text-search optimized; poor compression for metrics/flows.
pros: Mature, feature-complete platform (15+ years Elasticsearch lineage)
Excellent text search (log drill-down, regex, full-text anomaly queries)
Integrated alerting, SIEM rules, machine-learning plugins
Wide dashboard ecosystem (Kibana, Grafana plugin)
Tight integration with Security Onion, SELKS
cons: 3-4x higher storage overhead than ClickHouse for observability data
JVM-based; 4GB+ heap required (Pi-unsuitable; Proxmox-expensive)
Inverted index designed for text search, not time-series analytics
Licensing complexity (AWS dual-license model)
High operational overhead (cluster management, tuning)
technologies.fitForProject: Good if adopting SELKS (PostgreSQL backend) or Security Onion (Elasticsearch bundled). Less ideal if building custom — ClickHouse saves cost. Use OpenSearch Dashboards only if text search dominates use case.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox only. Minimum 8GB heap (16GB host RAM), high CPU. Raspberry Pi unsuitable.

technologies.name: Fluent Bit
technologies.summary: Lightweight (C-based) log processor and forwarder. <10MB footprint. OpenTelemetry native. Replaces Promtail (EOL 2026).
pros: <10MB memory; suitable for Raspberry Pi and edge deployment
OpenTelemetry OTLP native output; zero transformation to Loki/ClickHouse
Fluent filter language for lightweight transforms (grok, regex, JSON)
Multi-protocol input (syslog, TCP, UDP, files, systemd)
Promtail deprecation (EOL March 2026) makes Fluent Bit standard successor
cons: Limited to logs/events (not metrics or traces)
VRL language in Vector more powerful for complex transforms
Smaller plugin ecosystem than Logstash
Configuration can be verbose for edge cases
technologies.fitForProject: Excellent for Pi → Proxmox data pipeline. Deploy on Raspberry Pi 5 to ship Suricata EVE JSON to ClickHouse/Loki. Minimal resource overhead leaves Pi CPU for ntopng.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both. Pi 5: primary use (ship logs). Proxmox: aggregator instance collecting from multiple Pi/OPNsense sensors.

technologies.name: Vector
technologies.summary: High-performance (Rust) unified pipeline for logs, metrics, traces. Single binary; replaces Filebeat + Fluentd + Logstash. VRL language for sophisticated transforms.
pros: 10x throughput vs. Fluent Bit on x86 (Rust performance)
VRL (Vector Remap Language) powerful for complex parsing/enrichment
Single binary; unified metrics/logs/traces (not siloed)
OTLP, Prometheus, syslog, CloudEvents native support
Excellent for high-volume scenarios (1M+ EPS)
cons: Larger footprint (~50MB); marginal but noticeable on Pi
Steeper learning curve (VRL DSL)
Newer ecosystem; fewer specialized integrations than Logstash
Rust-based; different debugging model than Python/Ruby tools
technologies.fitForProject: Best for Proxmox x86 server collecting from multiple sensors (Pi, OPNsense, Suricata). Build sophisticated pipelines: ingest EVE JSON + sFlow + syslog, enrich with geolocation, fan-out to ClickHouse + Grafana Loki.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox primary. Fluent Bit better choice for Raspberry Pi due to memory constraints.

technologies.name: OpenTelemetry Collector
technologies.summary: CNCF standard unified collector for metrics, logs, traces. Moderate overhead; designed for standardized DevOps shops, not edge.
pros: CNCF standard (industry-wide adoption trajectory)
Unified metrics/logs/traces; vendor-agnostic
Extensive receiver/processor/exporter plugin ecosystem
Trace correlation built-in (W3C TraceContext support)
cons: Heavier footprint than Fluent Bit (~80MB)
Single ingestion point becomes bottleneck at scale
Configuration YAML verbosity (50+ lines for typical setup)
Less suitable for edge (Pi) due to resource overhead
technologies.fitForProject: Consider for centralized collection on Proxmox if already running OTLP-native services. Otherwise, Vector/Fluent Bit simpler for home lab.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox only. Too heavy for Raspberry Pi. Best as aggregation layer on Proxmox collecting from edge.

technologies.name: Grafana
technologies.summary: Industry-standard open-source dashboarding. Native plugins for ClickHouse, InfluxDB, Prometheus, Loki, OpenSearch. v11+ (2025) adds continuous profiling.
pros: 80% market adoption; extensive home lab documentation
Multi-datasource dashboards (ClickHouse + Prometheus + Loki in single panel)
Rich plugin ecosystem; ClickHouse datasource plugin (2024) fully featured
Free OSS edition suitable for home labs
Grafana Cloud optional for remote agent management (not needed for home)
Alerting, recording rules, provisioning via code
v11+ (2025) adds continuous profiling (bleeding-edge)
cons: Default dashboards for network security weak; requires custom building
PromQL knowledge required for advanced queries
Variable templating syntax obscure
Metric relabeling and label replacement powerful but unintuitive
technologies.fitForProject: Primary choice for visualization. Deploy Grafana on Proxmox. Build dashboards: ClickHouse for flow analytics, Prometheus for host health, Loki for alert/log correlation. Unify IDS telemetry across SELKS + sensors.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox only. Grafana server ~500MB-2GB depending on datasource count and dashboard complexity. Too heavy for Pi; use Pi to ship data, Proxmox for dashboarding.

technologies.name: OpenSearch Dashboards
technologies.summary: Kibana fork (Elastic 7.10 base); OpenSearch community project. Tight integration with OpenSearch cluster. Excellent for text log drill-down.
pros: Optimized for log search and drill-down (superior to Grafana for this)
Built-in alerting, anomaly detection, SIEM rules
Single UI for cluster health + log exploration
Kibana 7.10 features + community enhancements
Well-integrated with Security Onion, SELKS
cons: Tightly coupled to OpenSearch backend; poor support for multi-cluster queries
JVM-based; memory overhead similar to OpenSearch
Less flexible for metric visualization (weaker than Grafana)
Smaller plugin ecosystem than Grafana
technologies.fitForProject: Use if deploying SELKS (includes Kibana). Less ideal for ClickHouse-based builds. If using both OpenSearch (logs) + ClickHouse (flows), prefer Grafana for unified dashboards.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox only. JVM overhead; Pi unsuitable.

technologies.name: SELKS 10 (Stamus Networks)
technologies.summary: Turnkey Suricata IDS/IPS + Arkime forensics + threat-hunting appliance. June 2024 release. PostgreSQL backend; conditional PCAP capture. Targets home labs and small organizations.
pros: Out-of-box Suricata IDS/IPS with Stamus-maintained rulesets (2x/week updates)
Arkime v5.0 (2024) with JA4 fingerprinting, offline PCAP, bulk search
PostgreSQL backend (v10) replaces SQLite; production-ready scalability
Conditional packet capture; PCAP only for alerts (massive storage reduction 10-100x)
EveBox UI polished for security analysts; low learning curve (2-3 hours)
CyberChef + malware analysis built-in
Explicitly targets home labs; deployment options (ISO, Docker Compose, live USB)
Free, no subscription lock-in
cons: Elasticsearch backend not as efficient as ClickHouse for long-term storage
Limited customization vs. building from components
No native multi-tenancy
Stamus commercial NDR available but overkill for home lab
technologies.fitForProject: RECOMMENDED START. Deploy SELKS 10 as Proxmox VM (4 vCPU, 8GB RAM, 200GB). Provides threat detection + forensics out-of-box. Extend with ClickHouse for long-term analytics (not in SELKS). Bleeding-edge: Arkime 5.0 JA4 fingerprinting excellent for threat hunting.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox x86 only. SELKS 10 requires 64-bit x86-64; not ARM-compatible. Raspberry Pi: use as passive sensor feeding data to SELKS (ntopng or Suricata on Pi upstream).

technologies.name: Security Onion (Community Edition)
technologies.summary: Enterprise-grade NSM platform. Modular Suricata + Zeek dual-sensor. Ansible-based deployment. Elasticsearch backend.
pros: Dual-sensor (Suricata + Zeek) provides alerts + flow metadata in unified view
Highly customizable; Ansible-based provisioning
Wazuh integration for endpoint visibility
Mature community; extensive documentation
Supports 1-10Gbps depending on hardware
cons: Steeper ops learning curve than SELKS (network bridging, DNS config)
Elasticsearch backend storage overhead vs. ClickHouse
Ansible playbooks require Linux networking knowledge
More heavyweight than SELKS (more components to tune)
technologies.fitForProject: Good alternative to SELKS if you want more control over IDS/IPS rules and sensor placement. Better for multi-node deployments. For single Proxmox home lab, SELKS simpler.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox x86 only. Security Onion requires 64-bit; ARM unsupported.

technologies.name: CISA Malcolm
technologies.summary: Containerized network traffic analysis tool. Ingests PCAP, Zeek, Suricata alerts. OpenSearch + Arkime backend. CISA-developed, GH-hosted, Docker-deployed.
pros: Designed for home labs; 'easily deployable' in docs
Zero-config browser-based PCAP upload
Docker Compose (one command); platform-agnostic
Arkime + CyberChef built-in
Lightweight footprint (can run on modest Proxmox VM)
Apache 2.0 license; active development 2024-2025
cons: Passive analysis only (not live IDS/IPS blocking)
Requires PCAP/Zeek/Suricata data from upstream sensor (not standalone)
No native alerting or killswitch automation
Smaller ecosystem than SELKS or Security Onion
technologies.fitForProject: Best paired with live IDS (SELKS or OPNsense+Suricata). Deploy Malcolm for forensic analysis and incident response. Excellent for 'what happened?' queries after SELKS detects threat.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox x86 ideal. Malcolm Docker image x86-64; can run on Pi 5 but slow (passive analysis acceptable).

technologies.name: OPNsense + Plugins
technologies.summary: FreeBSD-based edge firewall; community-driven fork of pfSense. Weekly releases; no subscription lock-in. Suricata/ntopng plugins available.
pros: Virtualizes perfectly in Proxmox; NIC passthrough for WAN performance
Community-driven (no Netgate commercial pressure); weekly updates
Suricata IDS/IPS plugin native; ntopng traffic analysis plugin
Excellent gateway+firewall+IDS in one appliance
1Gbps throughput easily on modest CPU (2-4 cores)
Unbound DNS, OpenVPN, HAProxy, Nginx reverse proxy built-in
cons: Does not provide historical observability (requires external backend)
Suricata IDS performance (72% slowdown in user reports if misconfigured; good config needed)
Learning curve on rule management (less polished than SELKS)
Smaller ecosystem than pfSense (fewer third-party plugins)
technologies.fitForProject: Deploy OPNsense as Proxmox VM for gateway + firewall + IDS. Enable Suricata plugin for real-time blocking. Stream Suricata EVE logs to external ClickHouse/Loki for analytics. Pair with Malcolm for forensics.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox x86 only. OPNsense is FreeBSD-only (ARM unsupported). Do NOT use on Raspberry Pi.

technologies.name: ntopng
technologies.summary: Real-time traffic analyzer with L7 DPI. nDPI engine; PF_RING-based capture. RRDtool storage; ClickHouse integration (2025). Behavioral analytics.
pros: Runs on Raspberry Pi 5 (ARM support); minimal footprint (<100MB)
L7 protocol classification (nDPI) excellent for IoT/app identification
Behavioral analytics: lateral movement, periodic traffic detection
ClickHouse integration (2025, bleeding-edge) for long-term flow retention
Real-time UI updates; low latency (<1 sec)
SNMP, NetFlow, sFlow, IPFIX collector modes
cons: Not IDS/IPS (no signature detection or blocking)
Alerting weak compared to Suricata
Community edition limited analytics features (paid version more complete)
Smaller home lab community than Suricata
technologies.fitForProject: Excellent on Raspberry Pi 5 as passive sensor. Deploy alongside OPNsense (gateway) or SELKS (IDS). ntopng provides 'what is talking?' (protocol/app classification); SELKS provides 'is it malicious?' (signatures). ClickHouse integration (2025) enables long-term behavioral baselines.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Best on Raspberry Pi 5. Also works on Proxmox x86 but overkill (Suricata EVE richer data). Pi 5 can handle 1Gbps with ClickHouse backend.

technologies.name: Arkime
technologies.summary: Scalable, indexed PCAP storage and session forensics. v5.0 (2024) adds JA4 fingerprinting, offline PCAP, bulk search, multi-viewer.
pros: Indexes billions of sessions efficiently (Elasticsearch backend)
JA4 fingerprinting (2024, bleeding-edge); TLS handshake fingerprinting for C2 detection
Offline PCAP retrieval (forensics without live capture)
Multi-viewer for distributed PCAP analysis
Bulk search (2024); parallelized queries
Integrated with SELKS, Malcolm, Security Onion
cons: Requires Elasticsearch backend (storage overhead)
Passive analysis only (not IDS)
Complex index tuning for large packet volumes
Disk I/O bound (throughput limited by storage speed)
technologies.fitForProject: Use as forensic tool paired with live IDS (SELKS already includes Arkime v5.0). JA4 fingerprinting (2024) excellent for threat hunting post-detection.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Proxmox x86 only. Elasticsearch + Arkime too heavy for Pi. Use Pi as packet capture source; Proxmox for analysis.

technologies.name: Grafana Loki
technologies.summary: Log aggregation (labels-only indexing) from Grafana Labs. Label-based, not full-text search. Promtail shipper EOL March 2026; use Grafana Alloy instead.
pros: Index only labels (not full text); massive compression advantage
Low storage overhead vs. Elasticsearch (1/10th cost typically)
Grafana-native (tight integration)
Fluent Bit / Vector can ship to Loki via OTLP
Good for structured logs (JSON syslog, Suricata EVE)
cons: Promtail reaches EOL March 2026; migration to Grafana Alloy required
Label cardinality still matters (high cardinality slower than ClickHouse)
Full-text search weak (not designed for it)
Query language (LogQL) less powerful than PromQL
technologies.fitForProject: Good supplement to ClickHouse. Use Loki for recent log drill-down (7-30 days); ClickHouse for historical analytics. Migrate from Promtail to Grafana Alloy (2025) for unified metrics+logs+traces.
technologies.piVsProxmox: Both viable. Pi 5: lightweight Loki with 7-day retention. Proxmox: full Loki with longer retention + tiering.

bleedingEdge: ClickHouse ClickStack (2025): Unified logs/metrics/traces in single database, replacing ELK silos. 90% storage reduction vs. Elasticsearch for observability.
Arkime v5.0 (June 2024): JA4 TLS fingerprinting for C2/malware detection without payload inspection; offline PCAP retrieval without live capture; bulk search parallelization.
SELKS 10 (June 2024): PostgreSQL backend (production-grade) replacing SQLite; conditional packet capture (PCAP only for alerts), reducing storage 10-100x.
ntopng ClickHouse Integration (2025): Behavioral flow analytics directly into ClickHouse; long-term threat hunting baselines without indexing overhead.
Grafana Alloy (2025): Unified agent replacing Promtail (EOL 2026), handles metrics+logs+traces+profiles in single tool; reduces agent sprawl.
Vector VRL (2024-2025): Advanced observability pipeline language for Rust-based log processing; handles complex enrichment and fan-out without Logstash JVM overhead.
OPNsense Weekly Releases (2025): Community-driven firewall with bleeding-edge rules and plugins; no vendor lock-in vs. pfSense commercial drift.
Grafana v11+ (2025): Continuous profiling support; unified infrastructure+security+app observability in single pane; OpenTelemetry backend improvements.
rawFindings.recommendation: HYBRID ASSEMBLE-AND-EXTEND: Deploy SELKS 10 on Proxmox x86 as the foundation (IDS/IPS + Arkime forensics out-of-box). Extend with ClickHouse + Grafana for long-term flow analytics and threat trending. Optional: attach Raspberry Pi 5 with ntopng (or lightweight OPNsense) as passive sensor streaming to ClickHouse. This approach balances bleeding-edge tech (ClickHouse unified observability, Arkime v5.0 JA4 fingerprinting, ntopng ClickHouse integration) with proven appliance (SELKS 10) for minimal ops burden. Avoid pure build-from-scratch (Suricata rule maintenance + Arkime indexing + ELK tuning overhead); avoid pure appliance (storage cost, vendor lock-in, no long-term retention). Start with SELKS 10, add ClickHouse/Grafana, then iterate with ntopng on Pi for cost-effective passive sensing. DevSecOps wins: GitOps provisioning of ClickHouse schema + Grafana dashboards as code; automated killswitch via Grafana alert webhooks to OPNsense API.
openQuestions: What is the target network bandwidth (Mbps)? Home broadband (100Mbps-1Gbps) vs. gigabit LAN vs. multi-gigabit core? This determines Proxmox VM CPU/memory sizing and Pi viability.
Will you implement automatic killswitch (e.g., Grafana alert → block IP in OPNsense firewall) or manual alert triage? Automatic requires API integration testing.
Preferred flow data source: NetFlow v9/IPFIX from router, sFlow from network tap, or Suricata EVE + Zeek logs? This determines collector (InfluxDB vs. Vector vs. Fluent Bit) and schema.
Long-term retention requirement? 30 days (ClickHouse + Loki tier-1) vs. 1 year (S3 cold storage) vs. 7 years (compliance archival). Storage cost driver.
Will you run multi-node Proxmox cluster or single-node lab? Affects ClickHouse replication, Elasticsearch clustering decisions.
Acceptable learning curve for threat hunting? Home lab hobbyist (SELKS UI) vs. security engineer (custom Grafana + ClickHouse SQL)? Determines build vs. buy balance.
